#5801. NextEra-Dominion merger hearings kick off with focus on scope

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The case is “simply not the one to litigate the cost of service [or] who’s paying their fair share ... including the data centers,” said Joe Reid, an attorney representing NextEra and Dominion.

The proposed merger between Dominion and NextEra, announced in May, would create the largest regulated electric utility in the world, with a 130-GW large load pipeline. Clean energy groups, local Virginia officials and leaders of the state’s executive branch have raised concerns about the potential impact of the deal on rates and data center development.

McGuire Woods partner Joe Reid, representing the joint petitioners NextEra and Dominion, said the case “is simply not the one to litigate the cost of service, and nor is it the case to litigate who's paying their fair share and ensuring everybody pays their fair share, including the data centers.”

Reid noted that the proposed acquisition is a “consequential combination, but its size does not change the requirements of the Transfers Act or the analysis required to determine whether the statute's requirements have been met.”

SCC Chair Kelsey Bagot asked Reid if the commission “should not consider longer-term benefits in evaluating this proposed transaction,” and Reid replied that the commission “should consider all the evidence that is in front of it.”

Nate Benforado, a senior attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, argued that the Transfers Act is less narrow than the joint petitioners claimed.

“The analysis that the Utility Transfers Act requires is broad,” Benforado said. “Petitioners must prove that this transaction will not impair or jeopardize adequate service at just and reasonable rates … This is not simply a ‘do no harm standard’. This looks at virtually everything a utility does.”

Will Reisinger, representing the Piedmont Environmental Council, pointed out that the statute provides that “before approving this merger, the commission ‘shall be satisfied’ that adequate service to the public at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized.”

“That standard, satisfied, is subjective,” he said. “This is not a matter of calling a ball or a strike. This decision is 100% within your judgment, within your discretion.”

Will Cleveland, the attorney representing Google, said that the company plans to present testimony from energy economist Carolyn Berry, “who will testify that the minimum demand charge approved as part of Dominion's 2025 biennial rate case discourages large loads like data centers from taking advantage of their statutory right to retail choice.” Dominion has said “they don't think this testimony is relevant to the case,” Cleveland said, but Google disagrees.

Amazon’s attorney, Brian Greene, said that that company would want to see Dominion address two issues if the commission were to approve the transaction: “One is reforming the large load interconnection queue, and second is addressing the need for new capacity through bring-your-own options,” he said.

Greene said that Amazon proposes that “if the transaction is approved, Dominion be required to reform its study process through a cluster study approach that evaluates projects together and looks for coordinated system-wide solutions … Approving the merger without reforming the interconnection queue would be like putting more power behind the same undersized wire.”

#5796. The grid will fall short of AI’s power needs. These 6 resources can close the gap.

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

No single option is fast, firm and large enough on its own, writes Simon Irish, CEO of Terrestrial Energy.

Simon Irish is CEO of Terrestrial Energy, a developer of small modular nuclear reactors.

Most planning for artificial intelligence’s electricity demand starts with a forecast and asks whether it is right.

I would start somewhere else: Assume the grid will fall short, then ask how to close the gap — and how fast.

The evidence supports that starting point. McKinsey & Company estimates the U.S. will need 30 GW to 55 GW of additional capacity by 2030 as data center demand grows and aging plants retire. PJM Interconnection, the largest U.S. grid operator, has already seen the impacts of this trend. Its latest capacity auction fell about 6.6 GW short of its reliability requirement and cleared at the price cap.

Forecasts can be wrong, and requested load can be speculative or duplicative. But the PJM result is a market outcome, not a forecast. The useful question is which tools can close the gap, by when and at what cost.

The first four options below address serving data centers through the grid. The final two consider generation at or near the data center, with an optional grid connection. These categories overlap; on-site generation is a delivery strategy, not a generation technology, and can use multiple technologies.

Flexible demand. Duke University’s Nicholas Institute estimates the grid could absorb 76 GW of new load if that load accepted curtailment averaging 0.25% of annual consumption, in events of about 1.7 hours. It is the fastest option because it needs no new generation. It makes better use of capacity already on the grid.

But that capacity is finite, and beyond it, further load growth requires new supply. There is also a practical hurdle; to date, many data centers have shown little willingness to curtail AI workloads, because the value of computing far exceeds the cost of power.

Existing nuclear plants. Increasing output at operating plants through uprates and restarting closed plants can add reliable electricity supply, while extending operating licenses keeps existing plants running. A U.S. Department of Energy initiative targets 5 GW of added capacity at existing nuclear plants by 2029, and DOE has closed a $1.9 billion loan to restart Iowa’s Duane Arnold plant, returning 615 MW to service.

The limit is opportunity: Few operating plants remain candidates for significant uprates, and restarts are underway at nearly every plant where one is practical.

Natural gas. Gas offers firm power and a familiar path, but gas turbine supply has become the constraint. GE Vernova’s gas turbine backlog and slot reservations reached 116 GW at midyear 2026, and the company has said a heavy-duty turbine ordered today will not arrive until 2031. Buyers also take on fuel-price exposure and decades of emissions.

Wind, solar and storage. These resources can be deployed quickly and at scale. Their limit is that data centers require dependable power around the clock, so matching that requirement takes substantial overbuilding, energy storage and transmission infrastructure to deliver the same capacity as a firm resource.

On-site generation. Building a power plant at a data center can bring electricity online sooner by avoiding some grid upgrades and connection delays, where permitted.

However, it does not speed up equipment deliveries. An on-site gas turbine plant faces the same turbine shortages as one supplying the grid. Reliable operation also requires sufficient on-site backup capability or access to grid power during outages and maintenance. If a project relies on the grid, developers need clear terms defining that access and its cost.

Advanced nuclear energy. Advanced reactors offer firm, clean power and can be built as a fleet. They can serve data centers directly, with an optional grid connection. They will not close the gap this decade, and their real test is cost at fleet scale.

No single option is fast, firm and large enough on its own. Three principles follow.

Flexible demand, uprates at existing nuclear plants, and new wind, solar and storage can help meet near-term electricity needs.

Natural gas and on-site generation can help fill the gap while longer-term resources are developed, but only if equipment deliveries, permits and grid interconnection align with the data center’s schedule.

Advanced nuclear energy can contribute in the 2030s and beyond.

Utilities must plan now for both natural gas and advanced nuclear energy. DOE’s long-term modeling indicates 550 to 770 GW of additional firm, clean generating capacity could be needed by 2050, with advanced nuclear energy providing about 200 GW.

Infrastructure built to meet an immediate shortfall should also have a useful role later. A gas plant could provide firming capacity or operate during periods of peak demand as longer-term supply becomes available.

Make flexibility the price of speed. Utilities can offer earlier interconnection to customers accepting curtailment under defined, metered and enforceable terms. For data center operators, that is a choice between some power sooner and firm power later. Customers that can curtail load may get power sooner; those that cannot must wait for firm supply. This converts flexibility from an assumption into a contract and rewards developers whose flexibility is real.

Secure the long-lead items for firm, clean power now. Buyers who reserved gas turbine production slots early secured earlier deliveries; those ordering now may have to wait until 2031.

Firm, clean power has its own long-lead items, including fuel supply and equipment manufacturing capacity. Utilities and data center operators can sign reservation or offtake agreements that give suppliers the demand signal to build capacity before it is needed.

These principles also address the forecast debate. Some investments — flexibility, uprates and transmission — remain valuable across demand scenarios. Others are options worth buying, such as reservations for firm supply in the 2030s and beyond.

And some are bets to avoid: irreversible commitments sized to a demand number that may not arrive. If forecasts prove too high, the cost is the price paid to preserve an option. If they prove right and no one bought the option, the cost is the kind of shortfall PJM has already seen.

Planning for a shortfall is not pessimism. Of all the inputs AI needs, reliable power may prove the scarcest. The race to scale AI is a race to deliver power. Utilities, regulators and developers need tools that arrive on time, hold their value if forecasts change, and keep electricity reliable and affordable for existing customers.

#5793. Soneil Spark introduces its Mobile Battery Energy Storage System

This week, Soneil Spark rolls out its Mobile Battery Energy Storage System (Mobile BESS), the portable, modular battery storage built into a towable trailer.

The company, offering bespoke, modular energy solutions, is introducing Mobile BESS at RE+ 2026. It delivers temporary backup and off-grid power, working with what’s available by taking power from the grid, a generator, or solar.

“Wherever your business goes, the power goes with it. Simply tow it where energy demand grows,” said Sonya Jain, CEO of Soneil Spark, in a statement. “Start with one unit and add more as your needs change.”

It’s a simple set up, the company said. Mobile BESS works with no crane, no trenching, and no utility wait. That makes it a natural fit for a job site which may be months away from permanent service, a film set or event that can’t tolerate generator noise and fumes, a utility crew restoring power after a storm, or a remote mine or farm beyond the grid’s reach.

On sites that already run generators, the Mobile BESS syncs with them to cover peaks and start-up gaps, so the generators run fewer hours. Where diesel is restricted, it offers a quiet alternative.

Where containerized storage is built to be placed once, the Mobile BESS is built to be towed and to work in any weather. It includes:

The Mobile BESS is built for generator and equipment rental, construction, emergency and backup power, utilities, electrical contractors, events, film and entertainment, and off-grid sites such as mining and agriculture. A hybrid option adds EV charging.

#5783. New York state is short electric resources beginning 2033: ISO

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

New York will face an approximately 225 MW statewide resource deficiency, with the need for power resources growing to 1,850 MW by 2036, the state’s grid operator said Wednesday.

New York ISO’s 2026 Reliability Needs Assessment reveals the state’s increasing reliance on emergency operating procedures to maintain grid stability, highlighting the imminent resource shortfall. The ISO said it expects to call on demand response, voltage reductions, operating reserves, load curtailment and other measures, approximately 3.5 days next year, with that total growing to 21 days by 2036.

“New York’s reliability needs are no longer a distant concern,” Zach Smith, senior vice president of system and resource planning, said in a statement. “New generation and transmission resources take years to plan, permit, and build, so the reliability needs identified in this report must be addressed today.”

Along with the statewide resource deficiency, the report also identified local reliability needs. New York City is projected to be deficient by approximately 400 MW in 2032, growing to approximately 1,850 MW by 2036, while the Lower Hudson Valley deficiency grows from approximately 130 MW in 2032 to approximately 1,950 MW in 2036.

“While transmission investments can help address local reliability needs ... they cannot resolve the statewide resource shortfall,” the ISO said. “A combination of new generation, repowered resources, energy storage, dependable demand reductions, flexible large loads, and additional transmission will be required to maintain reliability over the next decade.”

NYISO expects demand growth of about 1,000 MW from manufacturing facilities and 1,700 MW from data centers will contribute to the shortfall. “The age and availability” of the state’s generation fleet is also a growing reliability concern, the grid operator said.

Approximately 4,600 MW of fossil generation will be more than 70 years old by 2036, according to the report. The assessment “accounts for this risk by projecting approximately 2,600 MW of generation as unavailable by 2036,” it said.

The ISO said it will continue to monitor the situation quarterly, reporting on the issue through its short-term reliability processes.

Once the 2026 RNA is approved by the NYISO board of directors, the grid operator said it will request updates to the base case “that may reduce or eliminate the identified reliability needs,” including changes in the status of generation and transmission projects, demand forecasts, demand response resources, large load assumptions and other system developments.

“If reliability needs remain after those updates, the NYISO will solicit and evaluate market-based solutions, regulated backstop solutions, and alternative regulated solutions” through the development of a 10-year reliability plan, the operator said.

#5775. Fuel constraints could challenge grid this winter, despite resource improvements: NERC

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Some areas in the Midwest, Southeast and New England could face resource shortages if transmission and pipeline constraints occur during periods of extreme weather, the reliability watchdog said.

Electric demand is growing, but “there has also been strong growth in resources,” Mark Olson, manager of reliability assessments, said Wednesday in a call discussing the outlook. “In many ways, the industry is on better footing going into winter this year,” he said.

However, Olson added that “historically, winter is the toughest operating period for the North American electric grid.”

While some models show the El Niño weather pattern can bring milder-than-average conditions that are a help to a constrained power system, “the reality is that extreme storms with ice and abnormal cold temperatures can lie within those averages,” Olson said.

“We're talking to our industry stakeholders about the need for extra vigilance. El Niño is a variable that adds to uncertainty for the winter,” he said.

Peak winter electric heating demand often coincides with higher residential gas usage, potentially leaving single-fuel generators that don’t have long-term gas contracts unable to show up when their generation is most needed, NERC officials said.

In the Northeast Power Coordinating Council’s Québec and Maritimes regions, “the supply can become strained during extreme winter peak demand,” NERC Senior Engineer Bob Tallman said on the call. “New England, as we've identified in the past several years, is assessed as elevated [risk] due to the constrained or limited gas pipeline infrastructure in that region.”

In the SERC Reliability Corp. East area, resources can fall short of extreme peak demand “during morning and low solar output periods of the day,” Tallman added.  And in the Southwest Power Pool and Midcontinent Independent System Operator territories, NERC identified subregions “where there are localized transmission constraints and it could be difficult to import into those areas if there was a wide-area winter event limiting local generation and increasing their reliance on imports.”

#5773. NAED Energy Holding Inc. Details the Rating of Its PV-1 Tandem Cell Line: 16,000 Wafers per Hour per Line, 4.6 GW from Six Lines

NAED Energy Holding Inc. (NAED) just published the rating of PV-1, its production line for T2X perovskite/silicon heterojunction tandem solar cells. Each PV-1 line is rated at 16,000 G12 half-cut wafers per hour: 400 wafers every 90-second index, a rate set by the line’s inline PVD tool (ITO-1). The line’s four PECVD modules are built for a faster 76-second index, about 18,950 wafers per hour.

At NAED’s planning basis—85% availability, 97.5% yield, and the T2X programme target of 30% cell efficiency—one PV-1 line produces about 116 million cells and 0.77 GW of tandem cells a year. NAED’s six-line site, at 96,000 wafers per hour, has a rated capacity of about 4.6 GW a year.

Throughput and capacity in this release are rated values, and cell efficiency is modelled. NAED will publish measured throughput, yield, and efficiency, with their test basis, as results are logged. For all technical information on PV-1 and the T2X cell, contact cto.fusion@naedcorp.com.

The 34.4% figure is NAED’s modelled T2X cell (Voc 1.969 V, Jsc 20.18 mA/cm², fill factor 0.867, 217.2 cm² half-cell). For context, the highest published efficiencies for perovskite/silicon tandem cells of this size are in the 32–33% range, including Maxwell’s certified 32.38% on a G12 half-cell reported in January 2026. NAED’s planning figures use the 30% programme target.

The comparisons below are rate-to-rate. A PV-1 figure describes a complete integrated line, while some benchmarks describe a single tool; supplier figures are the suppliers’ own published ratings.

A single PV-1 line runs at or above the rate of leading single deposition tools while carrying the full tandem process — wet clean, PECVD, PVD, top-cell deposition, printing and test — in one line. Six lines carry the output of about three large HJT lines or seven to eight commercial tandem lines.

One year of output from the six-line site is enough cells for about 7.7 million 600-watt panels, which would generate roughly enough electricity for about 650,000 U.S. homes for a year (17% capacity factor, 10,500 kWh per home; typical U.S. values, not site data). Panels keep generating for 25–30 years, so each year of production adds to that total.

#5771. OMCO Solar offers solar-powered tracker control system

OMCO Solar now offers a version of its OMCO Star Tracker Control System powered entirely by solar energy, allowing tracker controls to operate without AC power at the site.

The system, first launched last year, is designed for OMCO Origin Factory-Direct Trackers. Its tracker controllers, array controllers and sensor bridges use all-weather battery packs charged by solar modules.

According to OMCO, the technology eliminates the need for AC power to tracker control components and an uninterruptible power supply. It also allows tracker controls to operate and protects modules against wind, snow and hail before AC power is available.

“Our industry has solved so many problems as we have grown – we’re now the leading source for new electric energy capacity in the US. This addition to the OMCO Star product line solves one more – how to protect modules if there’s no AC power to the site even for a short time. We’re excited to offer this solution to our existing customers and to new partners,” said Matt Kesler, vice president of solar technology at OMCO Solar, in a statement.

The OMCO Star system uses LoRa, or long-range, wireless technology with a communication range greater than 1 mile. According to OMCO, this reduces the number of network controllers required and allows direct communication with every tracker without relying on a mesh network.

The company says LoRa is 100 times less susceptible to electromagnetic noise than Zigbee and better able to connect to distant trackers despite obstacles.

OMCO says its all-weather battery packs allow the solar-powered controls to operate reliably in cold climates. The system includes field-replaceable batteries, a phone app that eliminates the need for buttons on controllers and a remote monitoring and control portal.

The portal allows operators to move trackers for activities such as mowing, snow plowing and module cleaning. The system is developed, manufactured and supported by OMCO Solar in the United States.

“We are excited about bringing this innovation to the Utility Scale and DG tracker markets. Over the past few years, OMCO has expanded its capabilities beyond just being a US steel manufacturer to now being a true technology leader in our space. We look forward to supporting our customers/partners with the OMCO Star Tracker Control System, improving reliability, and reducing the labor and materials needed to build their projects,” said Eric Goodwin, vice president of business development at OMCO Solar.

OMCO Solar will display the all-DC tracker control system at RE+ in Las Vegas, November 17–19, in the North Hall, booth N516.

Washington, DC — Today and tomorrow, environmental and public health experts, alongside community advocates, will testify during a virtual public hearing to the dangers and risks posed by the Trump administration’s proposed rollback of long-awaited methane pollution standards finalized in 2024. The hearing is part of a broader public comment period in reaction to the Environmental Protection Agency’s plan to reverse key components of the landmark safeguards aimed at reducing methane, and associated pollution, from both new and existing oil and gas equipment.

Soon after taking office in 2025, the Trump EPA suspended the implementation of key provisions from the Biden-era standards, delaying their enforcement by up to 18 months despite no widespread evidence of compliance difficulties. Now, this rollback would permanently eliminate some of the rule’s most important safeguards, including its ban on routine flaring at oil wells and its program to leverage third-party monitoring data to identify and stop particularly large methane releases known as super-emitter events.

The proposal would also shield low-producing wells from leak monitoring requirements and other key safeguards, despite consistent evidence showing that such wells do not pollute less than higher-producing wells. Nearly one in ten people in the U.S. live in a county with over a thousand low-producing wells. These sources represent nearly half of the sector’s methane emissions and are primarily owned by large, well-resourced and highly profitable corporations.

Sierra Club experts and members will be among many testifying against the rollback.

In reaction, Sierra Club staff providing testimony released the following statements:

Andres Restrepo, Sierra Club Senior Attorney said: “EPA’s authority and obligation under the Clean Air Act to control methane emissions from the oil and gas sector has long been settled law, and the safeguards that the Biden Administration put into place in 2024 rely on cost-effective, widely available technologies and practices that the industry itself has used for years. The Trump Administration’s current proposal to strip the 2024 rule for parts and leave a rump regulation in place has support in neither the law nor the facts. The agency is attempting to manufacture sham justifications to mask what is nothing more than the giveaway that Donald Trump openly promised to oil and gas executives in exchange for supporting his campaign. Sierra Club will use every resource at its disposal to fight back against this betrayal of our families and communities.”

Cyrus Reed, Legislative and Conservation Director of Sierra Club’s Lone Star Chapter, said: “No state produces more oil and gas than Texas, and no state has more to gain from strong methane regulations than our state. We already have poor air quality from ozone pollution, particulate matter and other pollutants like hydrogen sulfide, and rolling back the methane standards will only make matters worse. Texas voters went to the polls in record numbers for a non-presidential election, and for the most part, voted for change, in largely because of anger over rising prices, but also due to a politics that often favor entrenched wealthy interests. This rollback proposal does not respond to this call for change, but instead proposes to let bad corporate actors off the hook and increase pollution that leads to higher energy prices, harms our health, and supercharges climate disruption.”

Antoinette Reyes, Permian Basin Organizer, Sierra Club Rio Grande Chapter, said: “As the federal government moves to weaken methane protections, New Mexico is working to strengthen its own. But pollution doesn’t stop at state lines, and neither should our commitment to protecting communities. Families in the Permian Basin already face industrial air pollution, from odors and poor visibility to respiratory health concerns. Every preventable methane leak wastes a valuable energy resource, potential tax revenue, and affects the quality of the air we breathe. Proven technology exists to reduce these emissions. State action alone cannot fill the gap left by federal rollbacks. We need strong protections at every level to safeguard our health, climate, and communities.”

Sarah Corcoran, Deputy Director of the Sierra Club Pennsylvania Chapter, said: “Pennsylvania is one of the leading states in the nation for fracked gas infrastructure. We are also one of the states with the highest pediatric asthma and cancer rates — but those numbers are increasing across the nation. The Trump Administration is not doing anyone any favors by reducing these regulations, not the industry, not the environment and not the American people who will feel the health impacts of these decisions for years to come. Policies that reduce methane waste, such as controls on flaring, quicker response times, transparent communications with impacted residents and more frequent testing are commonsense and cost effective. We need stronger protections in place for methane, not looser.”

Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that has more than 80 times the power of carbon dioxide over a 20-year period, driving approximately one-third of the warming our planet has experienced to date. Each year, the U.S. oil and gas sector emits large amounts of methane into our atmosphere. Methane is emitted from oil and gas sources alongside other damaging pollutants, such as smog- and soot-forming volatile organic compounds and air toxins like benzene and formaldehyde, human carcinogens.

According to EPA’s analysis, the 2024 standards are projected to avoid 58 million tons of methane through 2038, as well as 16 million tons of volatile organic compounds and 590,000 tons of air toxins.

#5768. PJM urged to delay base capacity auction until data centers cut from forecast

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

State ratepayer advocates and the grid operator’s market monitor say holding the auction in December as planned threatens grid reliability and could hit consumers with billions in unnecessary costs.

The request from the ratepayer advocates comes amid nationwide concern about energy affordability and data centers, as reflected in the midterm elections. The letter says that given “the urgency of the approaching auction,” its signatories request a written response from PJM’s board no later than Nov. 23.

In PJM, affordability concerns have been driven by a recent spike in capacity prices caused by growing data center load forecasts. PJM’s current capacity market rules effectively prevent data center companies from paying for their own power supply and infrastructure costs.

PJM recognizes the financial impacts rising electricity bills place on households and businesses, Jeffrey Shields, a spokesman for the grid operator, told Utility Dive in an email.

“The December auction includes an established price cap, providing an important safeguard against how high prices can rise,” he said. “The system urgently needs capacity to meet rising demand. Postponing the auction this close to its execution could destabilize the market and increase the risk of power interruptions when customers need electricity most.”

Electricity demand is growing faster than new power supplies can be built, according to Shields.

“While decisions about whether data centers and other large electricity users can connect to the grid rest with policymakers and utilities, PJM must plan for the demand those decisions create.” Shields said. “That means moving forward with securing the power we need while continuing to advance solutions that address the challenges of growing demand and the pressure on electricity costs.”

So far, including existing and forecast data center demand in PJM’s capacity market has increased capacity costs by $29.4 billion for all customers, according to Monitoring Analytics’ Nov. 12 report that called for the auction to be postponed.

PJM has responded to pressure from states, federal regulators and consumers by proposing a two-part plan to meet data center demand by facilitating bilateral contracts outside its normal capacity auctions, and also holding a backstop procurement for large loads that do not have bilateral contracts. It is also pursuing reforms to its rules for interconnecting large loads and generating supplies. The status of these efforts is pending.

The market monitor’s concerns were amplified by Exelon’s Nov. 3 complaint at FERC that challenged PJM’s three-year forward auction, partly over the uncertainty in forecasting data center load and the resulting billions in potential excess capacity costs, the ratepayer advocates said.

The advocates noted that PJM plans to publish the final “planning parameters” for the upcoming auction, which may remove canceled or delayed data center projects from the auction’s demand curve, on Nov. 19.

However, the market monitor’s recommendation is not simply to update PJM’s load forecast, they added.

“It is to fundamentally change how forecasted data-center demand is treated in the capacity auction so that existing consumers are not required to subsidize speculative or uncommitted data center demand,” the advocates said. “The delay would allow PJM to implement the IMM recommendations, subject to FERC approval and appropriate reliability safeguards.”

A “statement of principles” endorsed in January by PJM and the governors of its 13 states emphasized that large-load forecasts must be “real and verified,” the ratepayer advocates said. “Proceeding with an auction that incorporates both real and speculative data-center demand, despite the [market monitor’s] findings, would undermine that commitment and expose consumers to billions in potentially avoidable costs.”

The letter was sent to PJM by the Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel, the Delaware Public Advocate, the West Virginia Consumer Advocate, the Maryland Office of People’s Counsel, the Pennsylvania Office of Consumer Advocate, the New Jersey Division of Rate Counsel, the Illinois Attorney General’s Office and the Illinois Citizens Utility Board.

Richmond, Virginia — Tomorrow, November 17, the Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) will begin the evidentiary hearing for NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy’s merger proposal, which would create the nation’s largest ever utility. Sierra Club filed expert testimony last month urging the SCC to reject the merger given the way it threatens the Virginia’s Clean Economy Act (VCEA) and violates the Utility Transfers Act, posing a significant risk to energy affordability for Virginia families.

Dominion and NextEra have failed to show that customer benefits, not shareholders profits, were a motivating factor for the merger. If approved, the new utility would service 10 million customers across the Southeastern United States. Allied groups will rally outside the SCC tomorrow for the Stop the NextEra Takeover: Final Rally at the SCC.

Ahead of tomorrow’s hearing, Connor Kish, Director of the Sierra Club Virginia Chapter, issued the following statement:

“Throughout November, Virginians have shown up in droves at public hearings to oppose Dominion and NextEra’s proposed merger. Utility customers, independent policy experts, and local leaders have cited sky-high energy bills, AI data center demand, and abandoned climate goals as reasons to be wary of Dominion and NextEra’s bid to become the country’s largest ever utility.

#5765. Grid operators need data center ride-through rules that protect reliability

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The first facilities built to Texas’ new standard are about to come online, proving that firm, predictable regulation can protect reliability without slowing development, says ON.energy’s Alan Cooper.

Alan Cooper is CEO of ON.energy, a developer of power infrastructure.

On July 22, a mechanical failure forced a 230-kV transmission line in Northern Virginia offline. Within milliseconds, grid protection systems cleared the fault, as they are designed to do. The event would not have been a particularly noteworthy story, had it stopped there. It’s what happened next, though, that pointed to a growing challenge for grid reliability.

In response to the fault, data centers that had been drawing nearly 4 GW of energy, close to 4% of PJM’s load, collectively disconnected and switched to their on-site backup generation. The move sent voltage and frequency spiking across the system, a technically wonky but threatening result that caused power flickers as far away as Chicago. Thankfully, the prevailing grid conditions were strong enough to absorb the shock of the fault, so the grid held. But if the same event had hit Texas or even Northern Virginia at a time of higher demand, it could have caused a widespread outage. In West Texas, the Electric Reliability Counil of Texas estimates that a loss of as little as 3.2 GW could threaten grid reliability.

The power sector is not unfamiliar with the need for things hooked up to the electricity grid to “ride through” disturbance events. In 2023, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission told the North American Electricity Reliability Corp. to develop requirements that inverter-based supply resources like wind and solar facilities must follow to ensure they “ride through,” i.e., stay online, during certain disturbances. And this time around, NERC, FERC and several grid regions have been quick to identify a similar need for large loads to adhere to analogous standards.

In an Oct. 14 presentation to ERCOT, Dominion Virginia confirmed that the disturbance fell within the ride-through parameters that have now been finalized or proposed by NERC and two grid operators (ERCOT and PJM Interconnection). They concluded that if those requirements had been in place, the event would have been avoided.

Clear ride-through standards protect the grid, and they protect data centers’ ability to keep connecting to it. The open question for grid operators and regulators isn’t whether to create them, but rather which facilities the rules should cover. Some proposals would exempt projects that aren’t likely to draw grid power for years. Texas took a firmer line and in doing so, gave other operators and regulators an effective blueprint to follow.

The Public Utility Commission of Texas approved ERCOT’s ride through rule and it took effect in August. ERCOT made three choices that are key to making it work.

It drew the applicability line at energization. Facilities that energize roughly 18 months or more after ERCOT’s first market notice must comply with the rule. That exempts projects that are nearly finished, with equipment already ordered or even installed, and it applies to projects that exist only on paper, which can still change their electrical design for a small share of what a retrofit would cost later.

It measured the risk in exempt capacity within a cluster. ERCOT studies ride-through risk in its quarterly stability assessments. Those studies identify the clusters of large load that could trip together and the rule limits the amount of exempted load — i.e., the amount that is not equipped to ride through disturbances within each cluster — to 3,200 MW per single fault. Its latest results flag North Texas and Central Texas as active risk areas, with far West Texas being monitored.

It made the risk transparent and predictable. ERCOT watches each load cluster’s combined consumption in real time. When a cluster’s actual demand reaches about 2,500 MW, a mitigation plan kicks in: each utility and scheduling entity gets a “not to exceed” limit based on its share of recent peak use, and ERCOT keeps the authority to curtail non-compliant load. Because ERCOT publishes the study results and updates them over time, developers can see how much headroom is left long before they hit the limit. This transparency gives them time to decide whether to install ride-through capability, change their plans, or accept the risk of curtailment.

The result is that existing data centers keep running, and projects under construction generally avoid a forced redesign or need to buy different equipment. Other grid users stay protected. The first facilities built to the new standard will connect in the coming months.

In general, regulators and regional grid operators across the country are right to be careful about borrowing from ERCOT. Its isolated grid and energy-only market make much of its experience hard to apply elsewhere.

This isn’t one of those cases. A data center’s response to a voltage dip is the same in Virginia, Ohio or Texas, and so is the physics of thousands of megawatts disconnecting at once. NERC, PJM and other grid operators should adopt the core tenants of the Texas approach:

A single large-scale event would change the conversation overnight. Instead of debating exemption criteria, policymakers would be questioning if data centers can remain connected. Clear standards now are the best way to ensure the industry has a path forward.

The impact of a major event wouldn’t stop at the fence line: a multistate outage would affect the communities where data centers are concentrated and working to become good grid citizens. Proposed exceptions to ride-through requirements leave the door open for exactly the kind of event that consumers and policymakers are concerned about.

None of this protection is theoretical or depends on a technology breakthrough. Equipment to keep data centers connected through grid faults is commercially available today and already running in the field. The first facilities built to Texas’s new standard are about to come online, proving that a firm, predictable regulation can protect reliability without slowing market development. All too often, reliability problems are left lingering until there’s an emergency.

Large load ride through concerns can be solved now. The only thing missing is clear, consistent rules that protect grid reliability while providing certainty to the industry.

#5759. Trump Forces 7th Expensive Old Coal Power Plant To Stay Open

When a power plant gets old enough and is inefficient and expensive, it should be shut down. When it’s time to close, it’s time to close. As we’ve learned about the severe health costs and climate costs of old coal power plants, that’s even more obviously the case with them. But not for Donald Trump.

For some reason, Trump is obsessed with trying to bring the United States backward by several decades. That means, among other things, that he hates solar and wind power and he wants coal to rule again. Since coal power has become uncompetitive, he’s been using wacky logic to force old coal power plants to stay open while also paying off wind power companies to the tune of billions of dollars to not turn on power plants they’ve built. Trump’s logic with the coal plants is that we are in an energy emergency and urgently need the power — but aside from that being ridiculous, how can he then justify going and blocking wind and solar power plants from being finished and connected to the grid?

The Sierra Club updates us on this latest absurdity: “On Friday, November 13, the Trump Department of Energy issued yet another illegal ’emergency’ order, forcing the J.H. Campbell power plant to remain online. The Department issued that order despite the D.C. Circuit court ‘s decision in September rejecting the Department’s claim to ‘vast, top-down emergency power to pick its favorite generators to run at all costs.’

“This would be the power plant’s seventh order from the administration, despite no evidence that the plant has ever been needed to avoid a grid emergency or has ever prevented power outages. The extension order continues to cost families in the midwest region more than $600,000 per day to keep the old and toxic coal plant online.

“According to the Sierra Club’s Burning Money tracker, the Trump administration’s unlawful extensions have cost Americans well over half a billion dollars. Of that, over $326 million comes from J.H. Campbell based on reported utility cost recovery filings for portions of the facility’s extension orders.”

Half a billion dollars! At a time when Americans are struggling with high costs, Trump has forced expensive old coal power plants to keep running and has thus cost us half a billion dollars. And one wonders how a gigantic llue tsunami took over the country. Here’s more:

“At a time when prices are soaring and Americans are struggling to make ends meet, the Trump administration’s decision to issue yet another illegal and expensive extension is punishing,” said Sierra Club Senior Advisor Jessi Eidbo. “Families cannot afford to pay even more for electricity, especially when what they are paying for is a dated, defunct, deadly fossil fuel plant. The courts have already made it clear that these orders are illegal—ruling specifically that this very facility’s first order was not justified—but instead of listening to the courts and reason, Trump’s DOE marches ahead driving up costs to feed the coal industry. We will continue to challenge the administration until they stop.”

“Michiganders are growing tired of Trump’s attempts to keep them reliant on the dirty, expensive fossil fuel industry,” added Elayne Coleman, Sierra Club Michigan Chapter Director. “Michiganders showed up in droves on Election Day to reject this administration and seek something better. We look forward to working with our new leaders in Lansing and Washington DC, to expand clean, renewable energy in Michigan.” We’ll see. It’ll be hard to get any support for renewable energy through the White House as long as Trump lives there. We’ll see.

#5755. XPENG Forecasts 45% Sales Growth in 4th Quarter

XPENG just reported 3rd quarter financial details today, while also forecasting what will happen in the 4th quarter. Everything is looking quite rosy at the moment.

As far as 3rd quarter financials go, on the back of strong sales, the company logged 24.28 billion yuan ($3.643 billion) of revenue. That’s a new quarterly record for the company. It’s 19% more than in Q3 2025 and 23% more than Q2 2026.

That said, despite strong revenue, the company still scored a net loss. It had a significant 870 million yuan ($130.5 million) net loss, in fact, which was up 128% from 380 million yuan in Q3 2025 and down 35% from 1.34 billion from Q2 2026. XPENG made a small profit in Q4 2025, and since then has again been trying to get its finances into the green again instead of in the red.

Good news going into the 4th quarter is the company expects even better. XPENG is forecasting 169,000 to 174,000 vehicle deliveries, which would mean year-over-year growth of 45% to 50%. Expected revenue is 30.4 billion yuan to 31.8 billion yuan, which would mean growth of 37% to 43%.

We’ll see. The company is still not expected to get another net profit quarter, but perhaps the quarter could surprise and XPENG could log its second quarterly profit. One thing making that unlikely, though, is that XPENG’s R&D costs were up significantly, 17.5%. Also, general and administrative expenses were up 11.4% year over year. We’ll see what the 4th quarter brings.

#5752. BMW In South Carolina: A Free Trade Success Story

I recently attended BMW’s “Beyond The Machine” event in South Carolina. The largest facility of the German company globally is Plant Spartanburg in Greer, South Carolina. As part of the event, I saw the opening of BMW’s new battery plant in nearby Woodruff. We stayed in the nearby city of Greenville, which was transformed by BMW and the businesses that followed.

Beyond the vehicles and manufacturing, which I plan to cover in more detail in future articles, one of the most striking aspects was the human impact. From the “Woodruffian” Mayor fighting back tears at the opening of the battery plant to the plant employees to the people I met exploring the town, they clearly appreciate what BMW has done for the community. Throughout the presentations and discussions, there was support for free trade along with the local benefits. People in the area pride themselves in their resilience. They have reason to be proud. And they were optimistic about the growth of the increasingly clean manufacturing and electrified products from this global company.

The area around Greenville, South Carolina the rose to prominence in the 1870s on the textile industry. Cotton from throughout the South that had previously been shipped to other areas for processing was processed in Greenville and Spartanburg counties. However, as global competition increased in the 20th century, the mills became less competitive. The last textile mill closed in Greenville in 1977, although a few textile operations continued in the region into the 1980’s. As that industry left, the local economy declined. If the story ended there, many might use it as an argument against free trade.

When BMW came to South Carolina in 1992, they saw a lot of potential. Michelin had already started making tires there in 1978. Local leaders were enthusiastic to work with BMW. The people were also enthusiastic to receive training for the new jobs. The deep-water port of Charleston on the other side of the state facilitated shipping, while nearby rail links connected to much of the US.

Since 1992, BMW has invested over $15.8 Billion. The new Woodruff battery plant is their most recent major investment. In the process, an area that could have been considered a casualty of global trade became one of its greatest beneficiaries.

The first model, an E36 3 series, rolled off the line in 1994. BMW also produced the Z3 in the plant, including the first “German” car driven by James Bond on camera. However, the big breakthrough came with the introduction of the X5 in 1999. At the time, relatively few SUVs were being sold in Europe. BMW Spartanburg as the center of SUV production was intending to largely for the US. However, global markets shifted.

Now, Spartanburg is the “Home of X.” It currently produces the X3, X5, X6, X7 and XM, including electrified versions. It is the sole manufacturing plant for a number of those SUV models globally. A little over half of their production is exported, which also makes it consistently the top US overseas automotive exporter. Export volume topped $9 Billion in 2025 over roughly 200,000 X vehicles.

BMW designed those vehicles to be able to use ICE, PHEV and BEV powertrains. While some may want them to make just pure BEV, the approach gives BMW the ability to shift rapidly with the market. The different models also give the plant a level of market resilience. However, to fuel that resilience they need a very flexible supply chain that can respond quickly. Suppliers being close to the plant creates greater resilience.

BMW is designing its vehicles to be globally competitive. While 400+ miles of EPA range and charging speeds approaching 500 kW may be at the top of the US market, they are also competitive in global markets. While BMW developed the cells and packs, they use multiple suppliers to manufacture the cylindrical cells to their specifications. Packs at the plant currently use AESC cells, but they will shift to LG in the future and use other suppliers in other markets.

BMW also worked with the state of South Carolina to develop people. Nearby Clemson University provides a source of engineering talent, and BMW partners with the university on the Clemson University International Center for Automotive Research, where both students and BMW benefit from the development of new innovations. They are also developing potential future suppliers with the BMW Venture funds. One such company will be supplying flax-based composites to future M models.

A heavy emphasis is placed on technical training at the factory. In addition, they collaborated with community colleges to provide technical training. But the development programs start much earlier, with a heavy emphasis in middle school and sponsoring the First Robotics Competition for elementary school students.

BMW also worked with the South Carolina Department of Transportation to build infrastructure to support the plant and its suppliers. Moving forward, that infrastructure will increasingly include electrification and EV charging. BMW also worked with the SC Ports Authority to develop an “inland port,” which is essentially a direct rail link to the Port of Charleston. By moving freight by rail, emissions are greatly reduced. In addition, a lot of emphasis is going into transferring freight quickly, as every minute a truck sits idling is also wasted emissions.

While BMW employs 11,000 workers, over four times as many jobs are supported by the plant, according to a Clemson economist. That multiplier is much higher than most companies due to how BMW operates. Part of the impact on the local economy beyond employee count comes from the strategy behind the manufacturing. Overall, more than 70% of the value of the vehicles comes from outside suppliers.

Plant Spartanburg receives 3.3 million parts per day delivered by 1200 truckloads and 50 sea containers, 6 days per week. All those parts then go into over 1500 vehicles produced per day. The plant is laid out a bit different than some other manufacturing plants to facilitate the supply chain. Multiple fingers go up off the main line, along which parts are delivered to be assembled nearby. There isn’t much in the way of warehousing. Trucks come to the plant each day and the parts can end up on vehicles driving off the line the same day.

In the initial stages of manufacturing, more of the supply base came from overseas. However, as the plant established itself, more suppliers localized. That growing supply chain then attracted additional companies to the region, like Mercedes, Volvo and Scout. Those companies then create greater scale for the suppliers, who can reduce costs and expand operations.

Overall, for heavy, bulky components, localization will tend to  happen naturally. For a company that relies on suppliers to consistently and almost constantly deliver parts, that localization tends to increase. The more localized the supply chain, the more capable it becomes to respond to market dynamics. Once scale is attained for heavy, bulky components like batteries, that production will naturally become more localized.

BMW has a growing supply chain footprint across the Americas and especially across the Southeastern US. There will be over 850 Tier 1 supplier locations in the Americas by 2027, with multiple times as many Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers providing materials, parts and components. BMW focuses on value creation, competitiveness and collaboration in their supply chain. In addition, while they are bringing economic benefit, they are also focused on decarbonization.

Of course, all this economic activity has brought “green” in terms of money to the local communities. As I was stranded in Greenville due to flight interruptions, I had time to walk around the town and speak to some of the locals. Streets that were once desolate and unsafe are now vibrant with shops and restaurants. An area that people once wanted to leave is now growing rapidly and attracting people from around the world. I started conversations  with several friendly people in town about trade. I heard stories of transformation from past struggles to current successes.

Even though it was clear that they were benefitting from the economic impact, I was still surprised how strongly and openly they supported free trade and realized the benefits. A local guide pointed out major buildings and businesses that were new. Downtown is now pleasant and walkable. Part of that is due to the restoration of a river that runs through the city, surrounded by shops and artwork, where I saw some locals fishing in the clear water. This gets to the other kind of “green.”

While there are a lot of trucks transporting materials and components, shortened travel distances and efforts to streamline intermodal transfers reduce emissions. The proximity enables packaging to typically be sent back to the supplier to be reused. BMW is also putting a lot of effort into reduced CO2 emissions steel produced locally, which I plan to follow up on. Over half the steel in their vehicles is reduced CO2. Solar panels and landfill gas provide power for their facilities.

As the company relies heavily on its supply chain, the supply chain is a major focus of its decarbonization strategy. While EVs reduce emissions overall, the proportion of emissions from the manufacturing phase tends to be higher than for ICE vehicles, adding emphasis to decarbonization of manufacturing. At the same time, they strive to create regional strength, resilience and value creation while reducing emissions. Close collaboration is the key to meeting these goals. BMW plans to have net zero CO2 emissions throughout their supply chain by 2050 at the latest.

The new Woodruff plant will produce their sixth-generation battery. BMW develops the batteries first and then outsources the cell manufacturing, but they will now be manufacturing the packs locally. Initially, this will be for the iX5, to be delivered domestically and to global markets. However, additional EV models may benefit in the future.

Overall, politicians in the 1970’s could have tried to block global competition to protect the textile mills. That might have extended the life of those plants for a few years. However, in the process, those plants would become less globally competitive and less globally relevant. Protectionism would have only extended a slow, painful decline.

However, by keeping the market open and staying open to new business opportunities, Greenville, Greer, Spartanburg and Woodruff created the circumstances for their current success. People were open to new companies from other countries. They were open to industries that were new to the area. And they were open to investing in retraining to better take advantage of the new opportunities.

In the initial site selection, South Carolina could have imposed strict regulations and tried to force localization before the factory was built, production was ramped up and scale was attained to support that localization. If that happened, the plant would have undoubtedly been built elsewhere, and the economic benefits would have gone to someone else. By taking a more collaborative approach, rather than being confrontational, both BMW and local suppliers benefitted greatly. Building on that approach, more companies came to the region, building scale and amplifying the benefits.

BMW is not being hypocritical in their support of free trade. They are not promoting free trade just when it benefits them and then putting up barriers for other competitors. They are not shying away from global competition. They are seeking to make globally competitive vehicles for global markets. While global competition is fierce, by facing that competition, rather than hiding from it, their products become more competitive.

In the process, one of the brightest spots in US automotive trade globally, as well as one of the leaders in electrified product and supply chain decarbonization, comes from a German company.

Change and globalization can be scary things. Especially in the short term. The transition to EVs can also be scary, especially for those tied to the past. However, hiding behind political and trade walls rarely works out in the long run. A willingness to be open and collaborative with people who might come from within different lines on a map or sound different than you can have long term benefits. And the courage to engage with the technology transition and compete globally can put you ahead of many established competitors. That cannot only transform how we power our vehicles, but also transform the lives of people in communities for generations to come. As Woodruff Mayor Kenneth Gist put it at the battery plant opening:

BMW and the City of Woodruff wanted the same thing. Success in business, success in our community, and success in building the next generation of BMW electric vehicles to be the best in the world…

…When I think about this plant, I think about our children, our grandchildren. Educational partnership that will open the doors for them, the career that will be waiting for them, and a Woodruff they would be proud to call home for decades to come. BMW, you have been a true partner to me personally, to every person in this community.

Larry lives in Queens, NY, with his wife and cats. While he has spent much of his professional career leading global marketing efforts, his passions focus on clean technology and the automotive industry. He believes in Green Free Trade and the potential for the application of engineering talent to create solutions to the world’s most challenging problems.

#5750. Google signs 50-MW superhot geothermal PPA with Quaise Energy

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The agreement will support Google’s Oregon data center operations beginning as early as 2030, advancing development of a technology designed to access geothermal resources deeper underground.

Google's agreement with Quaise gives superhot geothermal an important commercial partner as developers seek to move enhanced geothermal systems from demonstration projects to utility-scale deployment.

“Geothermal energy remains largely underutilized. It supplies less than 0.5% of global electricity and is limited to just a handful of states in the U.S.,” Diane Hughes, senior vice president of marketing and communications at Quaise, said in an email.

Unlike conventional geothermal plants, which depend on naturally occurring underground hot-water reservoirs that are geographically constrained and rarely exceed 400 degrees Fahrenheit, enhanced geothermal uses engineered reservoirs to access heat in deeper rock formations.

Quaise is developing millimeter-wave drilling designed to ablate rock without mechanical contact. The company is designing wells to reach depths of up to 65,000 feet, where rock temperatures can exceed 932 degrees Fahrenheit and conventional drill bits cannot withstand the heat, according to Hughes.

“Superhot wells like these can produce up to 10x more power per well than what's currently in play and bring geothermal to places where it isn't viable or economical today," she said.

The agreement comes as technology companies increasingly seek firm power sources to meet data center demand. Google has signed nearly 35 GW of clean energy purchase agreements globally since 2010, including previous investments in next-generation geothermal, according to its most recent environmental report. Google says its three Oregon data center campuses are sourced with 83% carbon-free energy.

Google is also pursuing other emerging technologies, including advanced nuclear power and long-duration energy storage, as part of its efforts to achieve net-zero emissions.

Quaise said in its 2025 year-end update that it had drilled 118 meters through granite at its central Texas test site and is now working toward a depth of 1 kilometer.

#5749. The BLUETTI Apex 200 Expandable Portable Power Station — CleanTechnica Tested

BLUETTI continues to innovate, finding new ways to move its portable power station technology into meaningful new formats that provide owners with additional capability, portability, and utility.

They recently reached out about a new stackable portable power station format based around the Apex 200 power station. It packs in a meaningful 2.5 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of storage capacity by itself, but the real magic is that it was built to be modular and can be linked up with additional storage modules to be stacked underneath, connecting directly to the main unit.

Disclaimer: BLUETTI provided the Apex 200, B300K, and a pair of solar panels to the author for the purposes of this review.

This modular format is a game changer because it means you don’t need an installer to bolt 300 pounds of batteries to the wall of your house. Instead, you can order them in manageable formats and add more as you need them. Among other things, this capability allows the owner to assemble and disassemble the battery pack that meets their needs when they need it.

If you’re heading out to camp for a week in your RV, you can grab an Apex 200 and one of BLUETTI’s B300K expansion batteries and bring 5.5 kWh of capacity with you on the road. When you get home from the trip, you can put them back into the garage and add that back into the battery capacity for your home.

The BLUETTI Apex 200 serves as a head unit or master controller for the battery stack, while the other battery modules are effectively servants to it. For example, when you’re setting the unit up to charge from a wall outlet or from a set of BLUETTI’s solar panels, which can wire directly into the Apex 200 with MC4 connectors, you simply plug one set of connectors or one AC charging cable into the Apex 200 and it automatically balances the energy storage across however many additional battery packs are plugged into the unit.

That really simplifies the charging structure and allows you to use the battery exactly how you want to. If you want to just head to the park with two solar panels that are portable, you can do that and have a much more manageable power system, effectively bringing a mini-grid with you on the go.

We tested the BLUETTI Apex 200 out on a wall charger and, much like most of the other portable power stations on the market, it effectively maxes out the capacity you can actually draw from a wall outlet, which is around 1,600 watts continuous. Even with the best charging cables, you’re going to notice some heat building up in the cable, and BLUETTI has made some concessions for this. The Apex 200 has a switch that allows you to select from different charging modes:

When it comes to solar, the BLUETTI Apex 200 can plug in to solar arrays through either an XT60 connector or the MC4 connectors that wire directly into the unit on the side. Between the MC4 connectors and the XT60 solar input, the unit can pull down 3,000 watts of solar, though you will need to make sure the voltage on your panels lines up with what each of the ports on the unit can handle. When we initially wired our two Bluetti 100-watt solar panels into the unit, we had them wired in parallel, which resulted in just 40 volts being pushed into the unit.

Stacking them in series gave us 80 volts, which pushed it over the minimum 60 volts for the MC4 connectors and allowed the BLUETTI Apex 200 to start charging from the panels. Pushing 2,000 watts maximum of solar power into a 5.5 kWh battery stack is going to take some time to get it charged up, but it’s easy to manage scaling the input power system up to an impressive 2,000 watts to really deliver some meaningful power.

The flexibility is pretty impressive, because it means you can dial the system in to exactly what you need, whether that’s bolting an array to the top of your RV or installing solar panels on the side of your house and then wiring them in a way that’s the most convenient for you.

BLUETTI also makes a larger B500K battery, so you can really pick and choose exactly the right level of storage that you need for your house and the right size battery packs that you want to be able to move around.

The MC4 connectors for solar panels are a little bit troublesome on the BLUETTI Apex 200 because they require a special tool to release the locks that connect the male and female ends of MC4 connectors together. That means if you have your solar panels wired up and plugged into the unit, you’ll need an MC4 connector release tool to disconnect the solar panels from the Apex 200 before you move on. Alternately, you can wire the solar panels up through an XT60 connector, which is a simple plug-and-play adapter for lower voltage solar setups.

When it came time to use the stored power from the BLUETTI Apex 200 and the B300K battery pack, we had to pick up some more high-draw appliances to really put them the the test. We bought a 1,500-watt electric fireplace and 1,500-watt portable heater for a total draw of around 3,000 watts by. We also grabbed an an Instant Pot from the kitchen to pull a bit more juice from the battery stack.

The BLUETTI Apex 200 handled both of the heaters running full blast without a problem. It shared a continuous power output capacity of 3,200 watts. This gets bumped to 3,600 watts when you attach a B300K extension battery. Beyond that, you can even pull a little bit more power, pulling peak usage up to 4,800 watts for a few seconds, because of its peak power handling capacity.

Keeping the larger heater unit attached, we added an Instapot to the the mix, and again the unit had no issues no matter what power levels we used. It’s a solid stack with impressive stats that actually deliver when you need them to the most.

BLUETTI has really built an impressive system here with the Apex 200 and its different expansion battery options. A single BLUETTI Apex 200 can be expanded up to 33.3 kWh, and they can even go bigger than that if you need something with more storage.

BLUETTI allows you to link three Apex 200 battery stacks together through their Hub 1 accessory for a total of just under 100 kWh of storage capacity. That can be accomplished by stacking three Apex 200s with a bunch of BLUETTI’s 5kWh B500Ks and then linking them all together through the Hub 1.

It’s a massive system that shows BLUETTI isn’t just building products for a quick sale, but building a much more comprehensive, flexible storage system that you can build at home into the right configuration for your needs with components that act more like LEGO building blocks.

The ability to wire in solar via XT60 connectors and MC4 connectors is exciting, giving homeowners even more options to produce power from the sun for them to run their lives on. The BLUETTI Apex 200 retails for $1,399 USD.

For more information about the BLUETTI Apex 200, the B300K, B500K expansion packs, or their solar panels, head over to their official website.

#5748. GLP-1 Eye Warning Leaves Patients, Doctors With a Difficult Choice

— FDA should study outcomes when patients stop, continue, or change treatment after NAION

When someone loses vision in one eye while taking a GLP-1 drug, the first priority is an urgent eye examination. If the diagnosis is non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), the question that follows is: should we stop the drug?

On November 9, FDA announced it is requiring new warnings across all products in the GLP-1 drug class, which includes semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Zepbound, Mounjaro), among others, about a possible increased risk of NAION.

NAION occurs when inadequate blood flow damages the nerve that carries visual information from the eye to the brain. It can cause sudden, painless vision loss, often noticed on waking. The loss can be permanent, and there is no proven treatment to reverse it. The condition is rare, but these medications are widely used: in a March 2026 KFF poll, about one in eight U.S. adults reported currently taking a GLP-1 drug and one in five reported ever taking one.

As an ophthalmologist, I have routinely asked patients with suspected NAION about GLP-1 use for the past 2 years. I welcome the warning. The FDA should now pair it with a plan to study what happens when patients stop, continue, or change treatment after a NAION diagnosis.

People who develop NAION in one eye are already at increased risk of developing it in the other. How GLP-1 drugs might contribute remains uncertain. One hypothesis is that rapid reductions in blood sugar could cause swelling where the optic nerve enters the eye, compromising blood flow in susceptible patients. That possibility does not tell us whether continuing the medication adds to the risk in the other eye, or whether stopping reduces it.

These medications can be difficult to give up. Some patients take them to manage diabetes that has resisted other treatment. Certain drugs in the class also reduce the risk of heart attacks or worsening kidney disease in eligible patients. Stopping requires a plan for the condition being treated. When counseling patients who develop NAION while taking a GLP-1 drug, I recommend involving the prescribing doctor before changing treatment.

Regulators around the world have responded differently to this dilemma. European guidance says to stop semaglutide if NAION is confirmed. The FDA, whose warning covers the broader drug class, advises clinicians to consider discontinuation unless the benefits clearly outweigh the risk. I support that approach, with the patient, ophthalmologist, and prescribing doctor weighing the potential harm to vision against the benefits of treatment with a GLP-1.

Across 126 clinical trials, the FDA identified 15 probable NAION cases. The rates were equivalent to roughly six cases per 100,000 patients followed for a year among those receiving GLP-1 drugs, compared with four among those receiving a placebo or another diabetes medication. Larger observational studies have also raised concern, though their estimates vary and they cannot fully separate the effects of treatment from the conditions that led patients to receive it.

But estimating the risk of developing NAION does not tell us whether a patient should continue a GLP-1 drug after NAION diagnosis. One major FDA study excluded people with previous damage to the optic nerve from inadequate blood flow to help identify new cases accurately. That was a sensible design for its purpose, but it also means the study cannot establish whether continuing treatment after a diagnosis changes the risk to the other eye.

Some research has examined second-eye involvement. An analysis presented at the American Academy of Ophthalmology annual meeting this fall found that, among patients who developed NAION in both eyes, the second eye was affected sooner in GLP-1 users. It did not establish whether stopping would have prevented that outcome. Nor do we have reliable comparative evidence that switching to another GLP-1 drug is safer.

The FDA should assess whether its existing safety surveillance can answer these questions. If those systems fall short, the agency should require manufacturers to support additional studies. Federal law gives the agency that authority for serious safety concerns when routine reporting and available surveillance are insufficient.

The work could begin in participating eye clinics, linking confirmed diagnoses to prescribing and medical records. Researchers would document which medication a patient was taking, whether it was stopped or changed, when, and why. They would follow vision in the other eye alongside overall health, including how well replacement treatment managed diabetes or other conditions. Researchers would need to account for differences in diabetes severity and visual damage that affect both treatment decisions and outcomes.

The FDA should publish the study plans, identify who is responsible, and set dates for progress updates. Funding should be disclosed and results analyzed independently of manufacturers. Because NAION is uncommon, firm answers may take years. Patients and clinicians should still be able to see what is being learned and what remains uncertain.

The patient deciding what to do about the next dose cannot wait years for better evidence. Today's decision will have to be made with what we know. We owe that patient our best judgment, and we should follow what happens afterward. The next person facing the same choice deserves more to go on.

#5747. Groups Decry Trump EPA’s Decision to Grant Louisiana Oversight of Toxic Coal Ash

Testing at all Louisiana coal plants found unsafe groundwater contamination.

BATON ROUGE, La. — The Sierra Club, Earthjustice, and the Alliance for Affordable Energy Louisiana decried the Trump administration’s final decision today to put the State of Louisiana in charge of oversight of toxic coal ash waste. The Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality (LDEQ) has repeatedly allowed coal plants to violate federal coal ash protections.

Coal ash is generated when coal is burned, and massive quantities are stored at coal-burning power plants near Baton Rouge, Alexandria, and Shreveport.

At all three active Louisiana coal plants (Big Cajun 2, Brame Energy Center, R S Nelson), and the state’s one retired plant (Dolet Hills), monitoring data shows that coal ash is contaminating groundwater at levels above federal safe drinking water standards. These toxic chemicals include arsenic, boron, cobalt, lead, lithium, radium, sulfate, and thallium. More than 61% of Louisiana’s population relies on groundwater for all or part of their drinking water supply.

“Louisianans know all too well that we can’t trust our state regulators to hold polluters accountable, so it’s nonsensical that the Trump Administration just gave LDEQ even more authority to handle something as dangerous as coal ash,” said Darryl Malek-Wiley, a Sierra Club senior field representative in Louisiana. “It’s clear this decision is meant to favor wealthy coal-owning utilities at the expense of our health.”

“The Trump administration chose polluters over the people of Louisiana,” said Earthjustice senior attorney Mychal Ozaeta. “An alphabet soup of toxic chemicals from burning coal is contaminating groundwater in locations across the state. The right thing to do is make the polluters clean up their toxic mess, and protect sources of drinking water. Instead, the Trump administration is handing over authority to Louisiana’s state government which won’t lift a finger to clamp down on the concerning levels of contaminants poisoning the state’s groundwater.”

“Our state regulators are dangerously inadequate in their oversight and enforcement of polluting industries, which has already cost Louisiana our safe air and water. We simply don’t think LDEQ can handle even more responsibilities they won’t take seriously,” said Logan Burke, Executive Director of the Alliance for Affordable Energy.

Public interest groups submitted formal comments to EPA urging the administration to reject Louisiana’s request to handle coal ash oversight in the state.

Coal ash contains arsenic, mercury, chromium, lead, lithium, radium, and other heavy metals, which have been linked to numerous types of cancer, heart and thyroid disease, respiratory illness, reproductive failure, and neurological harm.

As an example of the state’s abysmal track record on coal ash, LDEQ has allowed power plants to close coal ash dumps with ash in groundwater, ensuring that the dumps will contaminate groundwater with toxic chemicals indefinitely. LDEQ should not be in charge of issuing permits that let coal plants continue to violate the law. These permits will shield power plants from federal enforcement and prevent Louisiana residents from stopping coal ash pollution.

LDEQ is a severely understaffed and extremely lenient environmental regulator. In addition to its coal ash failures, its air monitors are far away from Louisiana’s heaviest air-polluting facilities, and the agency has for years been criticized for approving permits for wealthy polluters, including LNG terminals and a massive Formosa plastics factory. Louisianans know all too well that LDEQ does not protect low-income communities of color, and creates a lax regulatory environment that has enabled disasters like the recent Smitty’s Supply explosion and spill.

Please see the Earthjustice Louisiana coal ash page.
