#5725. Should All Adults Be Screened for Lipoprotein(a)?

— Recent trial findings have provoked pushback of guidelines issued earlier this year

As a drug targeting lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), failed to prevent cardiovascular events in a closely-watched clinical trial, some experts are questioning recent national guidelines recommending that all adults be screened for it.

Back in March, a collaboration of 11 cardiology-related medical societies strongly recommended, for the first time, that all adults have their blood tested for Lp(a) -- also referred to as "Little a" -- at least once.

Higher scores, the committee said, reveal patients at much higher risk of developing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, incentivizing more aggressive management strategies, such as further lowering higher LDL cholesterol, HbA1c, body mass index, and other risks. The guidelines followed the European Atherosclerosis Society's similar recommendation in 2022 and the European Society of Cardiology's reinforcement in 2025.

But many prominent physicians say they are confused or are outright opposed to adding such a universal test. They argue that Lp(a), a heart disease risk marker known for years, is genetically inherited and not affected by LDL, diet, exercise or weight loss, and stays roughly the same through life.

They say the relationship to one's actual risk is unclear because Lp(a) may not necessarily be the cause of disease, but rather, may be related to something that is.

And there's not much one can do about a high score beyond what doctors normally recommend to reduce heart disease and stroke risks in their patients.

On top of that, CMS is allowing regional variation in whether Medicare covers the test, meaning that some seniors will have to pay for it out of pocket, depending on where they live.

"A lot of people are going to be very unnecessarily worried about a useless test that we should not be ordering or recommending in the first place," Rita Redberg, MD, MSc, a preventive cardiologist at the University of California San Francisco and former editor of JAMA Internal Medicine, told MedPage Today.

"It's certainly not going to make a difference in people once they pass age 50. You should be on a healthy lifestyle program no matter what your 'little a' is," Redberg said.

James Stein, MD, a cardiologist and emeritus professor at the University of Wisconsin in Madison, who has written several Substack blogs opposing universal use of the Lp(a) test, told MedPage Today the guidelines have "done a real disservice to the entire medical community by recommending widespread population screening because it creates a lot of anxiety."

"It also leads to a large downstream test cascade ... most of which is not indicated at all, and some of which actually puts you at additional risk for more problems," Stein said.

Then why did the committee make this recommendation?

"In general, there's been a 3-to-5-year push to do more Lp(a) testing, part of which is because there's a bias towards action. Let's do more. Let's prevent more disease," Stein said. "Part of it is because there's been some intellectual seeding, getting all of us ready for the Lp(a) lowering drugs, which a majority of people thought would show reduction in cardiac events."

In the HORIZON trial, the antisense oligonucleotide drug pelacarsen reduced Lp(a) levels, but it failed to reduce major cardiovascular events. That was a huge disappointment to researchers who had high hopes the drug would dramatically shrink cardiovascular death, strokes, and emergency cardiac interventions. If it had, it would have provided an important tool in the fight against cardiovascular disease.

But now, clinicians may find themselves at a loss for what to do about patients with a high Lp(a).

Stein remembers a recent clinic when three patients with no other cardiac risk factors "came in crying. Each one brought in a letter (showing their high scores)."

A woman in her early 70s had an extremely high score, above 350 nmol/l, with no family history and no other risk factors, and one of her children also had a high score, Stein said.

"'I can't believe I gave this to my child,' she told me," Stein said. "Now she is a healthy woman who feels like she has a sword dangling over her head. She does not."

Jason Goldman, MD, immediate past president of the American College of Physicians and an internist in Coral Springs, Florida, prefers recommending a coronary calcium CT score rather than an Lp(a), and was glad that at least the committee mentioned that option in its new guidelines.

"I am less enthusiastic about saying 'Little a' needs to be checked for everyone once because we don't have a treatment to lower it and improve outcomes, but we do have a treatment to lower LDL and cardiovascular disease," Goldman told MedPage Today. "CT calcium, I think, should be ordered on everyone, when appropriate."

He wishes the committee would reconsider its recommendation, especially in light of the HORIZON trial.

At the same time, several doctors told MedPage Today they welcomed the guidelines in their practices.

Jordan Rennicke, MD, a family medicine physician in Johnson City, Tennessee, orders Lp(a) draws for all his patients. And a few times, scores for patients without any risk factors including family history of cardiovascular disease have come back particularly high.

He knows that can "open up a can of worms," but he told MedPage Today he "values the information tremendously because then I can have a more informed discussion with my patients."

Karl Nadolsky, DO, an endocrinologist in Holland, Michigan, also checks all his patients. "It tells us who is carrying an extra inherited risk" that other scores don't show.

Roger Blumenthal, MD, chair of the guidelines committee and a Johns Hopkins cardiologist, said anticipation of positive pelacarsen trial results had nothing to do with the Lp(a) testing recommendation.

He said there's "overwhelming evidence from a multitude of studies that Lp(a) is a strong causal risk factor for atherosclerosis and aortic valve calcification and aortic valve stenosis."

The European societies' recommendations were particularly influential, he told MedPage Today. "We felt there are so many people who get cardiovascular disease at an earlier age than expected, and one common denominator is that they have a higher Lp(a). We felt it is a very reasonable test to do one time."

"Maybe some people say, well, you didn't have to have it as your strongest recommendation, you could make it a class 2A, and I certainly can understand that. But our colleagues across the pond have said the same thing ... that it's a good way to identify people who need to improve their lifestyle habits, that they may be at higher risk of atherosclerosis and aortic valve disease."

"And maybe we can do a better job of motivating people to improve their diet and exercise, and if you lower cholesterol significantly, you seem to neutralize most of the risk associated with a higher Lp(a)," he said.

Blumenthal emphasized that the "committee's guideline is not a rule. We're not saying that you have to do that. It's a simple blood test and it lets me know whether I take after my uncle or aunt who had a stroke or a heart attack at age 50. Then yeah, sure. Let's check it."

Blumenthal said in his own practice, he and many Johns Hopkins colleagues typically do not go by the new guideline to order Lp(a) blood screening for everybody. In his own practice, he orders it for patients who want to know their score, or if there's obvious risk factors like family history.

"There's a lot of well-meaning people on all sides," he said. "Some feel like if you measure anything, you're going to necessarily alarm people. But our feeling is that most people would like to know if they may have a factor that increases their risk, and if it does, then maybe that'll be the extra motivation."

"I understand there are other points of view and concerns," he said.

Among other historical exhibits, the museum commemorates the the Warsaw Uprising of 1943, known as the first — and for a long time the only — major urban battle against Nazi occupation during World War II.

After laying a ceremonial wreath at the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes at the museum, Newsom deployed his @CAgovernor account on X to underscore what appears to be the unifying theme of his campaign, calling the museum a “powerful reminder of fighting against the darkest forces.”

To kickstart the MOU, Newsom met with the leading Polish battery firm Impact Clean Power Technology. “Impact designs and builds batteries for electric and hydrogen buses, trucks, rail and industrial vehicles, as well as for mobile robotics, with a particular focus on humanoid robots,” Newsom’s office explains.

In a press release recapping the event, Newsom’s office also noted that the Governor told his audience that American voters “spoke loudly in the midterm elections,” in a reaction to “the Trump administration’s rampant corruption and embrace of Big Oil.”

#5723. Europe’s Inland Barges Need a Cargo Plan Before an Electric Fleet Plan

Coal throughput at Rotterdam rose 15.3% in the first nine months of 2026. Crude oil and petroleum-product volumes also increased. An inland vessel operator looking only at this year’s cargo market could see decades of work ahead. But an engine, battery conversion or replacement vessel bought now may still be operating in 2050, when the mix of cargo travelling through European ports and rivers will be different.

Rotterdam’s latest throughput release explains the coal rebound through recovering coking-coal movements, expensive natural gas and power-market conditions. Meanwhile, Eurostat reports that EU inland-waterway freight fell 3% in 2025 to 118 billion tonne-kilometres. Coal and crude-petroleum freight rose that year, while agricultural freight contracted. These changes are reshaping the services that ports, vessel owners and customers need to buy.

The Central Commission for the Navigation of the Rhine counted 6,224 dry-cargo vessels in Rhine countries in 2025, down from 6,410 in 2023. Smaller vessels account for much of the decline. Tankers moved the other way, rising from 1,400 in 2022 to 1,477 in 2025. The numbers describe a fleet already adapting to changing cargo and operating economics.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing on the inland barges Europe will need in 2050 uses a cargo-first model to work from the freight task to the future electric fleet. The underlying 98-page Inland Freight Electrification report is available to read.

A vessel owner has two connected capital decisions. The first is whether the freight service will still have customers through the useful life of the asset. The second is which propulsion and charging system can perform that service economically. Starting with equipment and then finding a market for it risks spending scarce investment capital on the wrong vessels.

I modelled a large European industrial port corridor from a 2025-style baseline to 2050. The central scenario assumes bulk cargo falls from 57.8 million tonnes to 34.4 million tonnes, a decline of about 40%. Wet bulk accounts for much of the loss, falling from 34.5 million to 15.0 million tonnes. Dry bulk declines from 23.3 million to 19.4 million tonnes. The model is a transparent scenario for investment decisions across this type of corridor, rather than a forecast of Rotterdam’s exact future cargo volumes.

The largest change is fossil-linked cargo. Fossil fuels and refinery streams fall from 19.0 million tonnes to 1.5 million tonnes, while coal and other solid fossil fuels fall from 2.5 million tonnes to zero. Combined, those reductions account for about 20 million tonnes of the scenario’s 23.4-million-tonne net decline. Any operator whose principal customers depend on moving coal or petroleum faces a different replacement decision from one carrying grain, construction minerals, chemicals or scrap.

Steel illustrates what cargo substitution means. The model reduces imported iron ore and other virgin iron units from 4.5 million tonnes to 3.0 million tonnes, while scrap and circular feedstocks rise from 1.8 million to 3.5 million tonnes. The industrial function continues as the materials moving to and from factories change. Existing barges and terminals may find new work, although parcel sizes, loading systems and routes will also change.

Biofuel feedstocks create a second trap. In the central scenario those movements peak near 5 million tonnes in 2030 before falling to 1.5 million tonnes in 2050. A temporary freight boom can support profitable operations without supporting a new vessel or terminal investment with a thirty-year life. The durability of the contract matters as much as the volume carried this year.

Cargo tonnage alone cannot size an electric fleet. The model translates commodities into powered vessel-equivalents using parcel sizes, routes, loaded calls and productivity. It starts with around 1,150 powered vessel-equivalents and ends with 664, a reduction of 42%. Dry cargo falls 17% in tonnes but 43% in powered vessel-equivalents because the modelled freight service changes. The starting 1,150 powered equivalents represent about 1,234 physical hulls after counting unpowered barges moved by pushers. Battery conversion decisions concern powered units; terminal and cargo-handling decisions also concern the additional hulls.

That distinction is particularly important for pushed formations. A pusher provides propulsion for several cargo barges. Converting one powered unit does not necessarily mean replacing every physical hull. Counting all hulls as propulsion conversions would inflate the equipment and financing requirement.

Low Rhine water levels bring a different constraint into the same calculation. A barge can remain on the register yet carry less freight per journey when draught is restricted. Cargo owners may have to buy more voyages, use different hulls or shift some freight to rail and road. Route depth, seasonal load factors and terminal access belong in the service model alongside cargo demand.

Ports should begin with a living cargo and route register showing which freight is declining, which remains, and which changes its material inputs. Vessel owners can connect that register to remaining hull life, annual utilization, cargo contracts and the cost of electric conversion. Utilities and terminal operators can then size grid connections, charging facilities and battery-container pools against vessels that will run on bankable routes. Infrastructure developed around dependable freight customers has a stronger prospect of earning a return.

Europe has good reasons to electrify established, high-utilization inland freight now. Battery-powered vessels are already serving container and bulk routes. The commercial opportunity is to invest in routes with surviving customers and electrify the services they will continue to buy. Expanding an electric fleet before measuring that freight task puts the order of decisions backward.

The complete TFIE Strategy Briefing works through the cargo substitutions, fleet denominator and investment decisions. The open Inland Freight Electrification report includes route-energy modelling, battery-pool sizing, terminal requirements and programme economics. TFIE Strategy also undertakes scoped corridor and fleet assessments for ports, operators and cargo owners.

#5722. Quadruple Agonist Reduced Weight Without Major Muscle Loss in Mid-Stage Trial

— Once-daily oral agent also showed favorable tolerability

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. -- An investigational oral quadruple receptor agonist led to substantial weight loss with preservation of lean mass, a randomized phase II trial presented here showed.

By week 13, the two highest tested doses of NA-931 -- 150 mg and 120 mg -- led to reductions in mean body weight of 13.8% and 11.3%, respectively, compared with a reduction of 1.9% with placebo among adults with obesity or overweight and weight-related comorbidities (P=0.001 and P=0.002).

Participants receiving the two lowest doses -- 60 mg and 90 mg -- lost 5.5% and 8.7% of baseline body weight, respectively, according to Lloyd L. Tran, PhD, of developer Biomed Industries in San Jose, California, and colleagues.

The topline findings "support the potential of NA-931 as a first-in-class oral quadruple receptor agonist for weight loss, with promising efficacy and tolerability," Tran said at the ObesityWeek annual meeting, adding that the results also "suggest potential muscle preservation."

Using dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) measurements, which estimate lean soft tissue, including skeletal muscle, organs, and water (though changes do not directly establish shifts in muscle function), lean mass decreased by 1.7% over 13 weeks among participants treated with NA-931.

For context, longer-duration trials of the GLP-1 agonist semaglutide (Wegovy) over 68 weeks and the dual GLP-1/GIP agonist tirzepatide (Zepbound) over 72 weeks reported reductions in lean mass of 13.2% and 10.9%, respectively. According to a 2025 meta-analysis of 22 randomized trials of semaglutide and tirzepatide, including 2,258 patients, lean mass reductions made up roughly 25% of total weight lost.

"We believe we are entering an era of post-GLP-1 where there is a need for sustainable obesity management" that pairs meaningful weight loss with preserved muscle strength, Tran said. That preservation is particularly critical for older adults, he noted, as muscle mass naturally declines by roughly 3% to 8% per decade after age 30 and accelerates after age 60.

NA-931 is a small molecule that targets four receptors: insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon. Because the compound readily crosses the blood-brain barrier, only a low dose is needed for efficacy, Tran explained, which may contribute to its favorable tolerability profile.

In the 150-mg NA-931 group, rates of gastrointestinal adverse events -- a common side effect of GLP-1-based therapies -- were only slightly higher than with placebo, including nausea (12.5% vs 10.3%; all cases mild), vomiting (8.3% vs 6.9%), and diarrhea (8.3% vs 6.9%). No participants in the 150-mg arm discontinued treatment.

By comparison, pivotal trials of semaglutide and tirzepatide reported nausea in 44.2% (vs 17.4% on placebo) and 24.6% to 33.3% (vs 9.5% on placebo) of participants, respectively.

This multicenter, double-blind trial enrolled 125 adults with obesity or overweight and weight-related comorbidities. Participants were randomized to receive once-daily oral NA-931 at 60 mg, 90 mg, 120 mg, or 150 mg, or placebo. Mean participant age across the groups ranged from 41.9 to 46.7 years. Most were female (62.5% to 66.6%) and white (62.5% to 68.9%). Mean baseline weight was 212 to 220.9 lb and mean body mass index was 34.4 to 37.8.

Patients in the 150-mg group also saw a modest reduction in HbA1c levels (-0.2%).

Tran said Biomed Industries is advancing NA-931 into phase III clinical testing.

ButyLok introduces a shoe-like component containing pre-applied, gel-like butyl material. When compressed by the G2 bracket, the material spreads across the intended sealing surface, potentially reducing manual sealant application and simplifying the installation process.

TRT is also introducing SAVRIX, another residential attachment option developed with manufacturing efficiency, installation practicality, and cost competitiveness top of mind.. Meanwhile, the RF-2 Rail Fastener is designed to simplify rail-to-bracket connections.

Top Rack Technology’s FreePivot Bracket features a 360-degree rotatable rail fastener and built-in height adjustment to accommodate varying rooftop conditions and simplify solar panel installations. Credit: Top Rack Technology

But perhaps the most versatile addition is the FreePivot Bracket. Its 360-degree rotatable rail fastener allows installers to accommodate attachment points that aren’t perfectly aligned. Built-in height adjustment helps compensate for uneven roof surfaces, while its all-metal construction supports durability. The one-orientation design and single-socket installation concept are also intended to reduce tool changes and keep crews moving.

Beyond the six new products, TRT is showcasing its established portfolio, including the TRT 01 Rail-less Base System, TRT 02 Rail-Base System, and TRT 03 Tile Hook System.

The company is also highlighting its Online BOM Design Tool, which supports project setup, structural design inputs, module layouts, engineering verification, and automated bill-of-materials generation. Connecting digital planning with physical mounting solutions could offer installers and distributors a more streamlined path from project design to field execution.

Installation hardware doesn’t need to be flashy to make a difference. Improvements in attachment flexibility, waterproofing, assembly time, and aesthetics can translate into meaningful operational advantages.

#5720. Why Car Trunks Matter Way More In GTA 6 Than Previous Games

After a 13-year wait and endless memes, the time has come for gamers of all stripes to call out of work for a few days and put their noses to the Grand Theft Auto grindstone. To put this in perspective, when "Grand Theft Auto 5" came out, the Tesla Model S was the best EV you could get had a range of 265 miles. Today, the longest-range EV SUVs are pushing past 400 miles. Before you put your headphones on and play for four days straight without coming up for air, though, there's something important you should know about how Rockstar's newest game works.

Car trunks are an integral component of how you'll plan missions and play the game. Why? Turns out, they're your best tool for managing inventory while on the go. Unlike in "Grand Theft Auto 5," where you had a functionally limitless inventory and could whip out your RPG on a dime and start blasting, it's looking like inventory management is going to be a big part of the gameplay in "Grand Theft Auto 6." You start the game with a set amount of stuff you can carry on your character, whether it's Lucia or Jason, and there's no way to increase that amount over the course of the game.

That's right. There's no raising skills or buying a larger carrying capacity, like in "Cyberpunk 2077." No trading Korok seeds for more slots, like in "Breath of the Wild." And certainly no princess treatment like an infinite inventory. What you see is what you get, and what you take into a mission is all you have. Thankfully, you can stuff a limited amount of gear into your ride's rear, allowing you a little extra flexibility while out exploring Vice City in your unlicensed, legally distinct Mercedes-Benz.

Taking full advantage of your trunk's inventory is mercifully easy. You just have to find where you parked your car (you parked in a designated space, right?) and open up your trunk, just like you would in real life. You can swap out gear you're carrying with gear stashed in the trunk, or you can keep your trunk empty, unload loot into it, and get back out to where the action is with inventory slots open for further finds.

If, for some reason, you decide to commit crimes while out enjoying a drive, you can clean up your mess by stuffing bodies in the trunk, too. You wouldn't do that, though, because you're a law-abiding citizen of Vice City, not a crazed criminal stealing cars and engaging in pointless police chases.

Your usable trunk isn't just handy for extra inventory, though. It could save your skin while evading the cops. Police in "Grand Theft Auto 6" are smarter than they've ever been (in-game, not in real life, obviously). When you get into trouble with the law, police NPCs will track certain characteristics of Jason and Lucia, which helps track these criminals across the city. They'll remember details like what clothes you're wearing, what weapons you're wielding, and what car you're driving.

You'll want to carry extra weapons and a change of clothes in your extra trunk storage. That way, when you get into trouble, you can run back to your car, complete a magical-girl transformation into your new outfit, and lower the likelihood that you'll get caught. Be careful, though. GTA 6 has Flock-like cameras that track your character's movements, and you'll have to stop at gas stations to fuel up virtually. So much for gaming being a break from reality.

GTA 6's usable trunk system promises to make the gameplay more dynamic and more challenging in fun ways, and it's a big departure from what franchise fans will be used to from "Grand Theft Auto 4" and "Grand Theft Auto 5." However, this isn't a completely original idea.

In fact, this is actually a reprise of a similar mechanic from an earlier Rockstar game. "L.A. Noire" is a 2011 neo-noir mystery game that also used a storage system that involved the trunk of the player character's car. Like GTA, "L.A. Noire" also features plenty of car chases and guns, though you play as a detective named Cole Phelps and try to solve crimes rather than commit them.

You may also remember a similar mechanic from the critically acclaimed and award-winning 2018 game "Red Dead Redemption 2." In "Red Dead Redemption 2," main character Arthur Morgan keeps a saddle on his horse that functions as additional storage. Much like in "Grand Theft Auto 6," returning to your horse allowed you to dig through your saddlebags and pull out both weapons and clothes, which are used to evade enemies and equip the different outfits needed for different weather.

For better or worse, inventory management is frequently one of the stickiest parts of game design, and it can make or break a game. Let's all cross our fingers extra hard that "Grand Theft Auto 6" nails the trunk storage mechanics and that changing your clothes in your car isn't a total drag like it is in real life.

#5718. Lamborghini Temerario Spyder Has Lambo's First Retractable Hardtop (And Its First Neck Warmers)

The Lamborghini Temerario has only been in the hands of customers for about a year, but the Italian automaker is already introducing a new version that will have a lot of owners rushing to their dealers to get the ball rolling on a trade-in. Say hello to the Lamborghini Temerario Spyder, which just made its world debut at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures. Lamborghini has been making droptop supercars since the Silhouette in 1976, but in this case it's actually quite behind the times — the Temerario Spyder is Lambo's first convertible with a powered retractable hardtop, a setup that has already seen its peak in popularity.

Still, this new model is quite exciting, and it definitely doesn't seem outdated. Lamborghini says the hardtop setup was chosen "to combine comfort, driving precision and aerodynamic efficiency," and its folding mechanism is unique to the industry. The best Lamborghinis are all about exuberance, and the Temerario Spyder seems to deliver that in spades.

There's not a ton to talk about from a styling standpoint, which is no bad thing. I already thought the Temerario looked awesome, and the Spyder looks even better. Its profile and roofline are largely the same, especially with the roof in place. There are two prominent cowls on the decklid just behind the seats, with a great set of trio of vents on each one, and in place of the coupe's smaller side quarter window is a new intake element. The engine cover does a nice job of showing off the V8 engine, and there are a bunch of other intakes, vents and aero elements adding visual interest. You can get a new livery option that adds a bunch of black accents to the interior, like sharp eyeliner around the headlights, and there are even more personalization options than what we've seen on the coupe.

Obviously the real star of the show is the roof, and its patented operating mechanism is unlike any retractable hardtop we've seen before. Instead of the roof sitting flat on top of the rear deck, it's split into two panels that stow vertically behind the seats, ahead of the engine. It uses ten electric actuators instead of needing the traditional electro-hydraulic circuitry, which makes it smoother to operate, quieter and more compact. It's fascinating to watch, especially when you look inside at all of the various components.

If the Spyder had a normal roof setup, the car's center of gravity would be 0.3 inches taller and 0.4 inches further towards the rear axle when the roof is down, but this vertical configuration means the center of gravity actually drops by a couple tenths of an inch when you open the roof, and weight distribution is unaltered. Lamborghini says it takes about 17 seconds to open the roof and 18 seconds to close it, and it can be done at up to 31 mph. If the roof is up, you can lower the rear window to be able to hear the engine roar without letting all of the elements in.

Lamborghini did a lot of work on developing the Spyder's chassis to preserve "the highest levels of structural rigidity and dynamic precision," and the Temerario was designed from the start with the Spyder in mind, so the company didn't have to make too many drastic changes. Compared to the Huracán Spyder, the Temerario has 6% more static torsional rigidity, 6% more dynamic torsional rigidity, and 9% more dynamic bending stiffness of the body shell. Spyder-specific suspension tuning is said to reduce secondary vibrations on uneven surfaces by 20%, as well.

Powering the Spyder is the same plug-in-hybrid setup as the Temerario coupe. It's got a twin-turbo 4.0-liter V8 engine that revs to 10,000 rpm (or 10,250 when using launch control), with the engine making 789 horsepower on its own. There are two axial-flux electric motors on the front axle and a third motor located between the engine and 8-speed dual-clutch transmission. Total output is 907 hp, just like the coupe, and it has 13 different configurations for the drive modes and hybrid system.

The automaker says the Temerario Spyder is about 220 pounds heavier than the coupe, and there's only a tiny decrease in acceleration performance to go along with it. The Spyder will sprint from 0 to 62 mph in 2.8 seconds according to Lamborghini, just a tenth slower than the coupe, and it's two tenths slower to 124 mph, needing 7.3 seconds to hit that mark. Not bad at all. It'll also reach a top speed of 213 mph, the same as the coupe.

Spec the Alleggerita package and a bunch of components will be made from carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer, like the front splitter, rear decklid and underbody panels. The door cards are also made from carbon, and if you choose the optional carbon-fiber wheels, total weight savings adds up to 49 pounds.

Lamborghini recently announced a new titanium Akrapovič exhaust for the Temerario coupe, which will of course be offered on the Spyder as well. Regarding the Spyder's sound in general, here's what Lamborghini has to say:

With the roof open, the sound of the V8 blends directly with the surrounding environment, while the adjustable rear window makes it possible to modulate the level of aerodynamic protection and the presence of the sound inside the cabin. The result is a more immediate and engaging experience, in which the progression of the engine is perceived by the driver seamlessly, while the sonic pulsations that accompany lift-off phases spread into the surrounding environment, amplifying the emotional character of open-air driving.

The Città, Strada, Sport and Corsa modes each retain a specific acoustic character. In Città and Strada, comfort and consistency of the sound response prevail; in Sport and Corsa, the V8's characteristic orders and the harmonics of the intake system are accentuated, accompanying rising engine speed with an increasingly intense sonic signature. With the roof open, this evolution becomes even more perceptible, turning the sound of the V8 into one of the most authentic expressions of Temerario Spyder's character.

As you're enjoying the wonderful sound, you can also enjoy a new neck warmer integrated into the seats, which has three settings and can reach up to 113 degrees Fahrenheit. The Temerario coupe is already much roomier inside than the Huracán was, and the same is true for the Spyder as well — Lamborghini says people who are 6-foot-7 can comfortably fit in the car, including when the roof is being opened or closed.

We don't know how much the Temerario Spyder will cost when it goes on sale in 2027, but expect to pay a premium of around $50,000 on top of the coupe's $382,000-ish starting price.

#5716. Tau Therapy Shows Continued Benefit at 2 Years in Alzheimer's

— Open-label extension data suggest diranersen's treatment effects may build over time

Diranersen, an investigational antisense oligonucleotide therapy that targets tau, continued to show benefits for 96 weeks, data from the open-label extension of the phase II CELIA trial suggested.

At 2 years, diranersen continued to slow clinical decline across measures of cognition, function, and disease progression, reported Lawren VandeVrede, MD, PhD, of the University of California San Francisco, at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease (CTAD) conference in Boston.

A 60-mg dose twice a year showed the largest effects; with that regimen, participants had a 1.09-point treatment difference in Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) score at 96 weeks, surpassing the 76-week CDR-SB score, VandeVrede observed. CDR-SB scores can range from 0 to 18, and a 1-point change is considered meaningful, he added.

Treatment effects were calculated by comparing 60 participants who received diranersen during CELIA's placebo-controlled phase and stayed on the same dose through 2 years with 115 people who were originally assigned to placebo and then moved into the study's open-label extension.

On the CDR-SB, the treatment effect grew from 26% at week 76 to 38% at week 96, VandeVrede said.

Other measurements of cognition and function also improved from 76 to 96 weeks, he added. "The increasing separation observed between 18 months and 2 years is remarkable," VandeVrede noted.

Safety findings through week 96 were generally consistent with data from the placebo-controlled period. The most frequent adverse events were procedural pain, post-lumbar puncture syndrome, headache, and confusional state. Most confusional state events were mild or moderate, occurred within 7 days of dosing, and resolved within 7 days of onset.

Diranersen targets microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT) RNA. It is designed to reduce both intracellular and extracellular tau.

CELIA was a phase II dose-ranging study of diranersen in individuals with early Alzheimer's disease. It enrolled 416 participants with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease or mild Alzheimer's disease dementia who had not previously received anti-amyloid therapy.

The study evaluated three doses of diranersen administered intrathecally over the 18-month placebo-controlled treatment period: 60 mg every 6 months, 115 mg every 6 months, and 115 mg every 3 months.

The primary endpoint was an assessment of dose response for change from baseline on CDR-SB scores at week 76. All diranersen doses tested in CELIA slowed cognitive decline, but because the lowest dosage performed best, the drug missed its primary endpoint of demonstrating a clear dose response. The ongoing open-label extension study is evaluating the long-term safety, tolerability, and durability of diranersen's clinical benefit.

"CELIA gave the field its first evidence from a randomized trial that lowering tau may slow cognitive decline, and today's 2-year data suggest that benefit may build over time," said Laura Nisenbaum, PhD, interim chief science officer of the Alzheimer's Drug Discovery Foundation in New York City, who wasn't involved with the study.

"The lowest dose appeared to perform best, but its safety and clinical benefit will need to be confirmed in a larger phase III trial," she noted. "Importantly, diranersen also lowered tau without affecting amyloid, making it a promising candidate to pair with anti-amyloid therapies as the field works toward combination treatments that address the full pathobiology of Alzheimer's."

New data from the placebo-controlled treatment period presented at CTAD showed that, at 18 months, the twice-yearly 60-mg diranersen group had favorable memory, orientation, and executive function scores compared with participants on other doses. Biomarker analyses showed that diranersen reduced tau PET signals and lowered soluble tau biomarker levels.

#5715. At $26,000, Would You Have The Last Laugh In This 1987 Corson Ferrari 512BBi?

Before you ask, no, today's Nice Price or No Dice 512BBi isn't actually a Ferrari. Instead, it's a Fauxrrari, one of 77 reputedly built by the Corson Motorcar Company on donor Pontiac Fieros. I know! You could have fooled me, too. Let's see whether buying this faker would be a foolish move.

First, however, let's look at what went down yesterday. When SCCA began the Trans-Am Championship Series in 1966, it was positioned as a more international-style road course competition, in contrast to NASCAR's wide oval shenanigans. Over the years, the series extended to tracks as far away as Canada and Puerto Rico. Today, the series' primary sponsor, Pirelli, maintains that international flair, though the number of competitions has been reduced and is now limited to tracks within the Continental U.S.

Starting in 1969, Pontiac celebrated the series by introducing the WS4 Trans-Am handling and appearance package on the company's F-body Firebird. Almost immediately iconic, that model served as the Firebird's performance vanguard until the model's demise in 2002.

Yesterday, we looked at a fairly unique Trans-Am, a 1997 convertible with the added-output WS6 ram air induction package and the promise of a well-cared-for life. While the comments were peppered with declarations that it wasn't the kind of car many of you would want to own, they also noted that the $13,000 asking price seemed in line with the description. Ultimately, that earned the Trans-Am a solid 66% 'Nice Price' win.

In the 1970s, the ubiquitous VW Type 1 Beetle served as the basis for many a home-built kit car. Dune buggies, classics, and swoopy sports cars emerged from the burgeoning industry, standing in for the original utilitarian sedan bodies. By the 1990s, however, the Bug was no longer available in sufficient numbers, and was reaching classic status on its own. That sent kit car companies to seek another platform to bend to their will.

That platform proved to be Pontiac's mid-engine Fiero, with its plastic body panels and monocoque steel chassis making the perfect canvas for all sorts of reimagining or imitation. It's that latter idea that we're looking at today.

That's right, today's 1987 Corson Ferrari 512BBi isn't the real deal. Ha, ha, fooled you!

Instead, this is a copy of that classic Pininfarina-penned Italian sports car, wrapped around the Fiero's mundane mechanicals and interior. And hey, it looks pretty convincing at first glance.

Built by Phoenix, Arizona's Corson Motorcar Company, the Fiero-based Ferrari homage was, in fact, far too close to the original in looks. That saw Ferrari successfully sue the faker-maker, resulting in the cessation of production and, rumor has it, the destruction of the company's molds. Something south of 80 Fieros were converted before the axe fell, including 5.7-liter V8 conversions and a small smattering of open-top Spiders.

This car, based on a 1987 Fiero, still has the stock 2.8-liter, 140-horsepower Chevy V6 sitting sidesaddle behind the driver, mated to a Getrag 5-speed manual. According to the ad, the engine has been updated with a "Custom exhaust" that the seller says "sounds great." Other notable features include a sunroof, cruise control, working A/C, and power locks. The (possibly fake) two-piece wheels look to be in great shape and are fitted with BFG tires that have plenty of life in them. An additional set of spinner-style center caps will accompany the car in the sale.

Looking at the car gives you an uncanny-valley feeling. From some angles, it's difficult to tell it from a real Berlinetta Boxer. From others, most obviously from the side, its proportions are sufficiently off to make the Fiero foundation obvious.

Like the real car, both the front and rear clips open fully for access to the spare and engine on either end. That likely made the fiberglass molding a lot easier as well. Other oddly real-appearing elements include the tail lamps, front grille and fog lamps, and the iconic orange turn signal panels on the nose. All the—questionably legal—badging is also present.

Inside the Corson, it's all Fiero, all the time. A Ferrari-badged steering wheel has been fitted in place of the original, along with a wood-veneer kit for the dash and console. Also, this must have been a GT or Formula back when it was nothing more than a Fiero, as it sports the ancillary gauge pod atop the center stack. Everything, inside and out, appears to be in great shape. The car shows 78,716 miles on the odometer and will come with a clean, obviously Fiero, title.

According to classic.com, the current average selling price of a real Ferrari 512BB is $290,242. The cheapest sale that site shows on record was $188,770, meaning even the deals aren't within the range of mere mortals. That's why cars like this Corson exist: to let the riff-raff like us get a taste of what exclusivity might be like.

At $26,000, this Corson 512BBi is a far cry from what a real car would cost, and it serves the added purpose of probably ticking off those who can actually afford a real edition or two. Who wouldn't want that?

A more important question is: who would want this fake Ferrari? What do you think? Is there a market for such a car, and does that $26,000 asking price put this car in play in that market? Or is that just too much for a game of "let's pretend"?

#5713. Biofuels in the EU Post-2030 Renewable Energy Framework

A deep-dive exploring the impacts of potential EU biofuels policy scenarios

The discussion around the future of the Renewable Energy Directive (REDIII) is underway as the European Commission devises what role renewable energy will play in transport in the post-2030 energy framework.

As the political priorities of the EU focus on energy independence and domestic industry, there is a renewed push for more first generation food and feed crop biofuels in the European transport energy mix. But these biofuels can have adverse impacts on the climate, environment and food supply chains.

To address these concerns, we have modelled three different policy scenarios to demonstrate the consequences of varying outcomes and their potential impact on the climate, environment and food security.

Our findings show that the current cap on first-generation biofuels set by the Renewable Energy Directive (RED III) can allow 72% more food- and feed-crop biofuels to be used in the EU transport energy mix, compared to what the bloc consumed in 2024.

When accounting for indirect land use change, even at current consumption, emissions from first generation biofuels already reach nearly 43 MtCO2e, about 23% more than the fossil fuels they replace.

When safeguards take the same form as stipulated in RED III and other key transport regulations, food- and feed-crop biofuel volumes, land-use area and emissions could all potentially double by 2040, emitting an equivalent to more than 5 million diesel cars.

In an unfavourable scenario, whereby the cap on first generation biofuels is harmonised at 7% across Member States’ transport sectors, volumes, land use and emissions would almost triple.

In a worst case scenario, where the cap on first generation biofuels is expanded beyond 7%, the negative consequences would be far heavier. We have used 10% as an example: volumes, land use and emissions could be four times today’s levels in 2040. Land dedicated to biofuels could reach 17.7 Mha, 18% of the EU arable land, an area larger than Greece, and emissions would exceed those of fossil fuels by 33 MtCO2e.

For advanced and waste biofuels, which are limited in supply, we show that the road sector is currently overconsuming available feedstocks, which should be directed towards sectors that cannot be electrified, particularly aviation. Furthermore, recent cases of fraud have highlighted the risks of relying on third country exports, making the case that all palm oil derivatives should be phased out and that effective safeguards should be put in place to allow for the most sustainable feedstocks.

Transport & Environment’s (T&E) vision is a zero-emission mobility system that is affordable and has minimal impacts on our health, climate and environment. Created over 30 years ago, we have shaped some of Europe’s most important environmental laws.

#5708. Mercedes-Benz's Point-To-Point Assisted Driving System Is Tomorrow's Co-Pilot In Training

One of my lingering concerns with any self-proclaimed autonomous driving system is losing control. Far too many times, I've fought lane-keeping assist through highway construction zones, but one automaker might have found the sweet spot: Mercedes-Benz is starting to roll out Point-To-Point Assisted Driving for its MB.Drive Assist Pro advanced driver-assistance system. The feature is impressive for a "Level 2++" system and lets drivers nudge their vehicles through precarious situations that would leave similar Tesla systems flustered.

MB.Drive Assist Pro relies on an extensive suite of eight cameras, 12 ultrasonic sensors, a mid-range radar, four corner radars, and, of course, a software stack co-developed with Nvidia. The semi-autonomous system doesn't rely on a cloud connection, leveraging an onboard high-performance computer capable of up to 254 TOPS, or 254 trillion operations per second. Mercedes has even grander ambitions in its sights with continued development of its SAE Level 3 MB.Drive Pilot system, eventual release of an SAE Level 4 system, and a robo-limousine ecosystem.

Full disclosure: Mercedes-Benz flew me out to San Francisco, California, and put me up in a hotel on the Embarcadero to experience its latest MB.Drive Assist Pro offerings and the bumper-to-bumper traffic over the Bay Bridge.

Point-To-Point Assisted Driving does what it says on the box. A driver can select a point in the navigation system and their MB.OS-equipped vehicle will drive them there. Over an hour's drive through the hilly, chaotic streets of San Francisco, I sat in the driver's seat of a Mercedes-Benz GLC EV as it safely navigated unprotected left turns and waited at stop signs for pedestrians to cross intersections. Sadly, the software hasn't quite got the California roll down yet.

The system operated exceptionally well, but it's not flawless. I had to intervene twice during the drive. First, the GLC misjudged the distance between a stopped bus and an upcoming intersection on a two-way street, and attempted to pass in the oncoming lane before sighting there wasn't enough room to slot in front of the bus. Second, the GLC detected a phantom stop sign and gradually stopped in the middle of the street.

This is where Point-To-Point Assisted Driving's best fallback came into play: you behind the wheel. In both situations, I was able to easily drive my way out without deactivating the Point-To-Point drive. The system encourages nudging. If your car comes to a stop at a non-existent intersection, you can simply tap the throttle and the car will continue on. You can also nudge the steering wheel to keep your distance from parked cars or puddles near pedestrians. Mercedes refers to the feature as cooperative steering.

While the Pro level receives point-to-point assisted driving, Mercedes also introduced hands-free highway driving for the mid-tier MB.Drive Assist option. MB.OS-equipped vehicles can operate semi-autonomously at speeds up to 85 miles per hour. The system also uses proactive lane changes so cars can maneuver into ideal lanes to approach exits and pass slower traffic; drivers can trigger lane changes themselves by using their turn signals. It honestly makes cruising down the interstate a breeze. I only had a slight scare when I got off I-880 and the car attacked the exit lane near the speed limit as traffic crawled in the adjacent lane. The software can be far more confident than a human, who would be wary of an impatient driver suddenly pulling into the exit lane.

It should be noted that both MB.Drive Assist and MB.Drive Assist Pro aren't truly hands-free, requiring the driver to touch the steering wheel occasionally. A typically green symbol on the dash will turn red, and if the visual warning is ignored, an audible beep sounds. Then, if there's still no contact with the wheel, the car will pull over and the Point-To-Point Assist will be soft-locked. The feature will only unlock and become available if the car is restarted.

It might sound extreme for Mercedes to lock a driver out of their vehicle's semi-autonomous feature if they ignore system warnings, but it's out of an abundance of caution. The German automaker wants to ensure that it has the safest software on the road, going above and beyond Euro NCAP and U.S. NCAP standards. On an empty dockyard in Alameda, Mercedes engineers set up a dummy-filled test range to showcase its suite of ADAS safety features.

Mercedes vehicles could react to pedestrians in traffic at a moment's notice. Automated emergency braking was still effective at highway speeds and avoided motorcycle riders darting from blind spots across the vehicle's nose. The software suite can even judge with steering away would be safer than braking. MB.Drive Assist comes with impressive creature comforts, like a 360-degree parking camera, rim protection warning, and parking and reverse assists.

These safety features are standard as MB.Drive on all MB.OS-equipped vehicles. MB.Drive Assist is optional on 2027 CLA, GLB, GLC, GLE and C-Class, as well as standard on the S-Class, GLS, and the AMG GT 4-door Coupe. MB.Drive Assist Pro is currently optional on CLA, GLC, GLE, GLS and S-Class, and the company claims that availability will be wider for the 2028 model year.

Mercedes has yet to reveal how much the optional subscriptions will cost vehicle owners. The automaker is rolling out the new systems in December with an early access program available to selected participants in California, Stuttgart and Munich, before nationwide rollouts next year through an over-the-air update.

#5707. FDA Approves First Treatment for Neurologic Symptoms of Type 3 Gaucher Disease

— Oral venglustat led to improvements in symptoms related to ataxia and cognitive function

The FDA approved venglustat (Infilbray) tablets as the first treatment for neurologic symptoms of type 3 Gaucher disease in adults and children weighing at least 15 kg, the agency announced Wednesday.

Gaucher disease is a rare, inherited lysosomal storage disorder caused by a deficiency of glucocerebrosidase. Without this enzyme, glycosphingolipids build up, mainly in macrophages in the spleen, liver, bone marrow, and lungs. In type 3 Gaucher disease, these lipids also accumulate in the central nervous system and lead to neurologic symptoms including cognitive deficits or problems with coordination and balance.

Venglustat is a novel oral glucosylceramide synthase inhibitor designed to cross the blood-brain barrier. By limiting abnormal glycosphingolipid buildup and its effects, it may help slow the progression of type 3 Gaucher disease.

"We have been able to treat the systemic manifestations of type 3 Gaucher disease, while the neurological manifestations remained beyond the reach of available therapies," Pramod Mistry, MD, PhD, of the Yale Lysosomal Disease Center and Gaucher Disease Treatment Center in New Haven, Connecticut, said in a news release. "The availability of a medicine capable of addressing the neurological manifestations of this devastating disorder represents a major milestone for patients, families, and the global type 3 Gaucher disease community."

The FDA's decision was based on data from the phase III LEAP2MONO trial, which compared daily oral venglustat versus intravenous infusions of the enzyme replacement therapy imiglucerase (Cerezyme) in 43 patients ages 12 and older. Study participants had previously achieved stabilization of their systemic manifestations with enzyme replacement therapy. At 52 weeks, a global test of multiple neurologic endpoints showed that venglustat achieved significant improvements in symptoms related to ataxia and cognitive function (P=0.0137).

The most frequently reported side effects with venglustat included gastrointestinal symptoms and adverse effects on mood, the FDA said. "Serious psychiatric risks, including suicidal ideation and behavior, have been reported," the agency pointed out. "Potential risks identified from animal studies include potential clouding of vision in younger patients and adverse effects on fetal development when drug is taken during pregnancy."

Prescribing information includes warnings and precautions for suicidal ideation and behavior, lens opacification in pediatric patients, and embryo-fetal toxicity.

The open-label phase of the LEAP2MONO study is ongoing and results will be presented when available, drugmaker Sanofi said.

#5706. The Return Of Project Hail Mary … And Next Steps For Artemis, Too

Word has just dropped that the mega-hit sci-fi film “Project Hail Mary” has returned to the big screen for the holiday season with its nail-biting tale of science, adventure and friendship. Catch a brand new Hail Mary trailer on YouTube while the action heats up here on Earth, including solicitations for the next class of astronauts, the formation of the new US Space Academy, and next steps for the Artemis mission to the Moon.

On November 7, NASA (the National Aeronautics and Space Administration) began taking applications for the next class of astronauts. The deadline is 11:59 PM ET on December 3.

NASA received more than 8,000 applications during the last round of astronaut recruitment, in 2024. Only 10 candidates were selected — but don’t be discouraged. Just look at the payoff as described by NASA:

The next generation of astronauts will train to operate on the lunar surface, live and work beyond Earth, and take on missions that will push the boundaries of human exploration farther than ever before.

“The next generation of astronaut candidates could help write history while inspiring future scientists, engineers, and explorers,” adds Scott Tingle, chief astronaut and chair of the NASA Astronaut Selection Board. Interested? Apply here.

If you blinked, you missed the formation of the new US Space Academy. However, the folks over at the Louisiana Economic Development agency were on the ball. On November 12, LED announced that Louisiana has thrown its hat into the ring for the privilege of hosting the the forthcoming Space Academy.

“The Space Academy is a proposed NASA-supported federal academy that will educate the next generation of astronauts, engineers, scientists, and leaders for America’s space programs,” LED explains.

If all goes according to plan, the first Space Academy class will occupy Louisiana State University in New Orleans with a roster of 300 students in the fall of 2028, with room for a total of 4,000 — or more — to follow.

If you’re wondering why Louisiana thinks it has a good shot at hosting such an endeavor, Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry summarized the case in a press statement. “The United States Space Academy belongs in a state that builds the rockets, supports our nation’s military and is now home to the world’s largest spaceport,” Landry enthused.

As described in an LED press release, the state’s qualifications include hosting “America’s Rocket Factory,” aka the Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans. The facility is owned by NASA and managed by the Marshall Space Flight Center, which among other projects has just released a new album of “baby star sounds.”

The idea of a dedicated center for space education and training bubbled up from the White House just a few months ago, in August. NASA promptly jumped on it, inviting the governors of all 50 states to compete for the new facility.

Louisiana is determined to beat them all to the punch. With LED in the lead, collaborators on the state’s Space Academy proposal include Louisiana State University, the City of New Orleans, the business organization Greater New Orleans, Inc., and the New Orleans subsidiary of the leading utility Entergy among others, with all of the state’s US Senators and Representatives enlisted in support.

“A dedicated state fund, the Louisiana U.S. Space Academy Fund, will cover startup needs and independent operating infrastructure, lowering the federal investment needed to launch and sustain the Academy,” LED adds, noting that two other schools — Southern University at New Orleans and Tulane University — are also lending their support to the LSU campus.

LED and its partners are leaning heavily on the presence of the Michoud Assembly Facility to leverage its claim to host the Space Academy. As LED notes, Michoud has been front and center in crewed space flight for 65 years, and it sits only about nine miles from the LSU campus

“Michoud built the Saturn V first stages for Apollo, every Space Shuttle external tank, and the core stages for the Space Launch System rockets that power NASA’s Artemis missions,” LED explains.

“The National Center for Advanced Manufacturing at Michoud develops the composite and metallic manufacturing processes behind that hardware,” the agency adds.

LED Secretary Susan B. Bourgeois also chipped in her two cents. “Louisiana is building one of the most consequential aerospace ecosystems in the country, and the U.S. Space Academy would give us the opportunity to build the talent pipeline alongside it,” Bourgeois said.

“Cadets would learn alongside leaders in government and commercial and space, including NASA’s Michoud Assembly Center and Stennis Space Center, SpaceX Starbase Louisiana, Michoud tenants including Boeing, Lockheed Martin, Textron Systems, and Vivace,” LED elaborates, also taking note of the presence of the Naval Information Warfare Center among other resources.

“Greater New Orleans anchors the middle of America’s southern space corridor, which runs from Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral to Johnson Space Center in Houston and SpaceX’s Starbase in South Texas, with Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville to the north,” LED adds again for good measure.

As for the Artemis mission, as of October NASA seemed pretty optimistic about the chances for sending people to the Moon sooner rather than later. A new schedule calls for an Artemis III test flight in Earth orbit next year. The flight will include shakeouts of docking and other systems between NASA’s Orion spacecraft and lunar landers from both from SpaceX and Blue Origin.

“Four astronauts will fly aboard Orion, launched on NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, for a planned 14-day mission in Earth orbit to reduce risk ahead of the Artemis IV moon landing mission,” NASA explained.

“The Artemis III mission will unfold in sequence,” NASA explained. “Blue Origin will launch a Blue Moon lander test article into Earth orbit, SLS will launch Orion and its crew, docking with the Blue Moon lander test article, then SpaceX will launch a Version 3 Starship lander test article while Orion will undock from Blue Moon and dock with Starship.”

Assuming that all goes off without a hitch, 2028 will see US astronauts on walking on the Moon, presumably before anybody else gets there.

The last time US citizens set foot on the Moon, millions of Terrestrials witnessed the fuzzy, flickering action on live TV. If you were among them, share the experience in the discussion thread What was it like? Did everyone cheer? Or did somebody say something random such as “I need a cigarette,” and is that the moment that burns especially bright in your memory? Asking for a friend…

#5705. GM Prepares For Life Without CEO Mary Barra

Good morning! It's Thursday, November 19, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition, General Motors is trying to figure out what its world without Mary Barra in it would look like, over 1,500 Rockstar employees are voting on whether to unionize as Grand Theft Auto 6 goes live, German automakers are staring down the barrel of a work stoppage as a labor fight takes hold and Ford has started shipping the battery cells it's building in partnership with China's CATL.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

Mary Barra has been the CEO of General Motors for nearly 13 years at this point. For some, it's hard to think of modern GM without her, but with her 65th birthday just a month away, folks within The General are clearly starting to do so. The automaker is working with an executive search firm to look for possible outside candidates to succeed Barra as it prepares for a future that'll come once the highest-paid Big Three CEO hangs it up. Don't worry, current GM employee, the company is also looking at internal candidates.

Barra has apparently been laying the groundwork for months to hand over the keys to the company. She's already GM's second-longest tenured CEO — beaten out only by its first CEO, Alfred P. Sloan, Jr., who was in the position for 23 years. Still, her tenure is about twice that of the average modern CEO of an S&P 500 company, and she's the first woman to run a global automaker. So far, GM hasn't indicated publicly when Barra could step away from her post. From The Wall Street Journal:

GM has historically groomed chief executives from its own ranks, and internal candidates remain in the mix. Contenders have included the company's finance chief Paul Jacobson; Sterling Anderson, a high-profile Silicon Valley hire who serves as Chief Product Officer; and Mark Reuss, a 40-year GM veteran and Barra's No. 2, according to separate people familiar with the matter.

Barra took over as GM was still rebuilding after its 2009 bankruptcy and has led the Detroit automaker through trade wars, the global pandemic and tumultuous forays into electric and autonomous vehicles.

GM's stock, up 25% from a year ago, has risen about 136% since she took the reins, and the company has returned tens of billions to investors through sweeping buybacks.

Barra took over with a mandate to shake up the automaker's notoriously hidebound corporate culture. Her GM has emerged as a smaller but more profitable automaker anchored by its lucrative U.S. truck business.

GM is selling millions fewer vehicles around the world than it was a decade ago, after retreating from unprofitable foreign markets while slashing low-margin sedans and other slow sellers in the U.S. Yet it is generating record levels of cash and turning bigger profits despite fewer sales.

The company has spent the past decade trying to pivot away from its roots as a traditional car manufacturer and instead remake itself into a software-driven tech enterprise—a push marked by a string of Silicon Valley hires, an expanding California hub and heavy bets on autonomous driving and digital services.

Of course, not all of Barra's gambles have worked out. GM lost billions on its Cruise robotaxi division before pulling the plug, and its original electric vehicle plans have been a bit of a disaster that cost the automaker $6 billion in write-downs. WSJ also notes that several of the high-profile tech hires it made saw relatively short tenures.

Barra and GM are clearly playing things close to the chest. Just a few months ago, the CEO was asked if she's considering stepping down, and she told Fortune magazine that she remains energized.

"I still feel like I can contribute and continue to build the foundation," she told the outlet.

We'll see how long she continues, but the $48.2 million in realized compensation she made in 2025 certainly helps.

Unless you're at Patrick Star's house, you're aware that Grand Theft Auto 6 launched at midnight, and it's one of the biggest video game releases ever. In preorder sales alone, GTA 6 generated over $1.6 billion in revenue, and that number is sure to climb as folks buy it in the coming days. Even with all that immense amount of money, workers at Rockstar, the studio behind GTA, don't think they're getting their fair cut. That's why over 1,600 Rockstar employees in the UK are voting on whether to form a union, and if it wins recognition when the ballot closes on November 26, the Rockstar Games Workers Union would be the largest in the UK gaming sector.

In an op-ed for The Guardian, Rockstar animation programmer and union representative Nestor Uriarte said the studio's reason for a unionization push is because of a decade-long realization that "to tackle the industry's mounting challenges we need to come together." He argues that union recognition would help safeguard the working conditions of developers who built GTA 6 over the past decade. From PC Gamer:

"Behind these numbers are thousands of people whose talent and hard work make the games possible. With a recognized union, we can ensure everyone, across every department, sees a fair share of the success we contributed to," Uriarte said. "Our games are industry-leading. Our wages, conditions and bonuses should be too."

Working conditions at Rockstar produced one of the early flashpoints in the advancing push for games industry unionization over recent years, sparked by employees' descriptions of its "death march" crunch culture and allegations of sexual assault. While the studio's taken steps towards a healthier workplace in the years since, employees have reported continuing concerns around gender pay gaps, crunch, and nebulous bonuses conditions.

Coinciding with the union vote, a Glasgow tribunal is weighing testimonies in the ongoing legal battle around Rockstar's alleged union-busting and firing of employees who had been involved in organization. Meanwhile, just days before a launch that's projected to earn landmark revenue, Rockstar parent company 2K reportedly laid off a third of the employees at XCOM and Civilization developer Firaxis.

"It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off," Uriarte said. "But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised."

"We've heard from colleagues who are nervous that the union is an outside troublemaking force that will threaten the company," Uriarte said. "But we're not outsiders. We are hundreds of studio employees who live for Rockstar, its output, and the players. We want to see it succeed."

Uriarte said that recognition would also provide developers with a greater ability to negotiate the rapid proliferation of AI in game development, which represents an existential threat to workers in an industry where one third of the labor force has been laid off in the past two years.

Audi and BMW are among the German automakers that are facing 24-hour strikes this week after workers approved industrial action. It's the latest escalation in an intensifying nationwide dispute over pay, benefits and working hours at a time when automakers are already under pressure caused by weak demand, high costs and stiff global competition. Employees are seeking greater flexibility in labor costs and working hours, and the IG Metall union is pushing for higher pay and commitments to project investment and jobs at domestic factories. From Bloomberg:

IG Metall will halt production Friday at Audi's main Ingolstadt plant and BMW factories in Munich, Dingolfing and Landshut, it said Thursday. Workers at sites operated by Robert Bosch GmbH, ZF Friedrichshafen AG and other industrial firms in Bavaria are also set to walk out for a full day.

In northern Germany, IG Metall has already secured backing for 24-hour strikes at selected plants across Bremen, Hamburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Schleswig-Holstein and northwestern Lower Saxony.

Major companies in the region include Mercedes-Benz Group AG, which operates a large vehicle plant in Bremen, as well as aircraft manufacturer Airbus SE and shipbuilder TKMS AG & Co. KGaA, though the union hasn't identified which sites will be targeted.

The union has offered to allow companies to deviate from collective agreements in exchange for commitments to invest in German plants and secure products and jobs, according to IG Metall. Employers haven't taken up that proposal, the union said.

IG Metall is demanding a 5% pay increase and higher apprentice wages in Bavaria, and it claims that employers have proposed no permanent increases for the first 20 months, following by a 1.3% raise. That's, uh, less. They're also looking for greater scope to cut special payments and extend working hours.

This wouldn't be the first such action. Over 118,000 workers participated in an earlier wave of short strikes in Bavaria through last week. The 24-hour walkouts are the first such escalation by IG Metall during a wage round since 2018.

As I was just saying, solidarity forever.

Ford has started producing its lower-cost battery cells at a new plant in Michigan that are meant to be used in its upcoming Fathom electric pickup truck. The central Michigan facility is owned by Ford, but it uses technology licensed from Chinese battery maker CATL, which hasn't sat right with some lawmakers and officials.

The prismatic-shaped cells made at the Michigan plant have a lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) chemistry, and they're going to head to Ford's plant in Louisville, Kentucky, to be fitted to Fathom prototypes. From Reuters:

Several automakers are transitioning to LFP chemistry because it ​costs less than nickel-based batteries and is considered more durable.

US ​Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote in a September letter to ​Ford CEO Jim Farley that his agency was "deeply alarmed" by Ford's reliance on ‌licensed ⁠technology from CATL at its plant in Marshall, Michigan

Ford called the letter a "wrongheaded attempt to capture headlines," and touted its development of a US battery plant while other automakers continue to ​import batteries from ​China.

Ford's Alan Clarke, ⁠vice president of advanced development projects, told media this week that working with CATL was the ​fastest way to build affordable electric vehicles in ​the US. "CATL ⁠being the biggest in the world, it means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ⁠how ​to produce LFP cells," he said.

Seemingly undeterred by the Trump administration's foolishness, Ford says it will be able to make 40 cells every minute at the battery facility, and a spokesperson for the company expects them to still be eligible for a federal battery manufacturing tax credit.

#5704. Star of 'The Pitt' Teams With Scrubs Maker to Wipe Out Medical Debt

— Noah Wyle says the initiative is "half philanthropy and half protest"

Noah Wyle, who stars as Dr. Michael "Robby" Robinavitch on "The Pitt," is teaming up with scrubs maker FIGS to relieve $200 million of medical debt.

Wyle and FIGS are each donating $1 million over the next 3 years to the nonprofit Undue Medical Debt, which buys up medical debt for pennies on the dollar. Wyle and FIGS' contributions are expected to relieve the debt of about 150,000 Americans.

The first round of people will be alerted that their medical debt is wiped ahead of this holiday season, the partners announced.

"This is an act of half philanthropy, and half protest, to underscore what the need is, and see if we can't get our arms around some better solutions," Wylie told CNN.

Wyle said he stumbled upon the debt-erasing organization last year and was impressed by "how much you could do with a little bit of money and have it go a long way."

Undue Medical Debt buys portfolios of medical debt, with each dollar spent erasing about $100 in medical debt. Afterwards, patients receive a letter letting them know their debt is no longer owed and they don't have any lingering penalties.

Americans have a whopping $220 billion in medical debt, which is carried by approximately 1 in 3 people, the companies said. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has called medical debt crisis "a uniquely American phenomenon."

Wyle told CNN that while the average amount of medical debt carried is not a lot, "it's enough to keep you in poverty. It's enough to make you defer going back to the doctor to get the treatments you need, or to make really difficult choices between heat and healthcare, food and healthcare."

In previous interviews, Wyle revealed that the upcoming season 3 of "The Pitt," which takes place in the winter, will explore some of these hard choices that patients have to make between healthcare and other basic needs.

Last season, the show tackled the looming, life-altering influence that medical debt can have on patients' lives. One patient checked out of the emergency department against medical advice. He was uninsured and already had $100,000 in medical debt that he had been hiding from his family

Even when his doctors made it clear that he was putting his life in danger by leaving, and went above and beyond to secure the patient a discount from the hospital, he couldn't bear to bring on any more medical debt, and left. Spoiler alert: that same patient returned to the emergency department later that day in even worse condition.

This storyline highlighting the real impacts of medical debt and how it shapes patients' decisions was heart-wrenching for viewers, but also for the fictional emergency department physicians on the show who couldn't do anything to get their patient the care he needed.

"Trust is the bedrock of the relationship between patients and clinicians like nurses, pharmacists, and doctors, and that trust is increasingly undermined by the burden, and even fear, of medical debt," Undue Medical Debt's CEO and president Allison Sesso said in a press release.

"On the other side of January, with the 'Big Beautiful Bill,' a lot more people are going to find themselves without health insurance, which means going out of pocket for these kinds of things and incurring more debt," Wyle said on CNN. "It's kind of an unsustainable system, and it's one that really needs to be addressed."

#5703. These Are The Cars You Want Robert Pattinson's James Bond To Drive

Robert Pattinson is James Bond. It's an unexpected casting, but likely a good one — Pattinson loves to get weird with a role, and that's exactly what Bond needs after the gritty Craig movies. Every Bond movie needs a Bond car, though, and we haven't yet seen what Pattinson will drive in his first outing in the role. That's why, earlier this week, I asked you all what car Robert Pattinson should drive as Bond. Today, we're looking through your answers.

Some of you picked genuinely good spy cars, like a beat-up Nissan Altima. Others went for more of the Mr. Bean approach with an Aston Martin Cygnet. Still some of you appear to have just stepped out of a 20-year coma, and only know Pattinson from "Twilight" rather than "Primetime," "The Odyssey," "Mickey 17," "The Batman," "Tenet," "The Lighthouse," "Good Time," or any other movie he's been fantastic in since his last appearance as Edward Cullen 14 years ago. Let it rest, y'all.

Should be a Volvo C30, because it would be a full circle from the first Twilight movie and that would amuse me.

We can incorporate driving a classic car into the plot. First he drives that new electric Jag with all the spy features, lasers, mines, machine guns etc. Then it gets hacked and driven off a bridge and Bond almost dies. After recovering, he drives a DB5 that can't be hacked.

Has to be an Aston Martin. Needs to be unique and stylish, but also manage to blend in when needed.

2014 Altima complete with damaged left quarter panel and duck taped rear bumper. No one will ever know he's a spy.

In this day and age? An Uber. Don't want to attract attention by driving the same car past Flock cameras all the time.

James Bond is usually reflective of his era. Sean Connery was peak cold war and peak Mad Men era. Pierce Brosnan was lighter, post cold war who looked and acted like a 90s banker investing in pre-tech crash stocks. Daniel Craig was the Global War on Terror Bond, a bruiser who could have back back from two tours in Afghanistan.

Robert Pattinson is the post GWOT Bond. From looking up pictures of him (I had no idea who he was until they announced it) he's less built up and less brooding than Daniel Craig, probably closer to a Pierce Brosnan Bond. I'd expect more sophistication (a British prep school backstory, not an orphan with a murky past), less hand to hand combat, probably more tech forward than Daniel Craig's Bond.

Bad guys will either be AI, Russia (a Putin analogue) or a combination of the two. It won't be China because Amazon will want to sell tickets in China/stream in China so it'll have to get past Chinese censors.

So expect the new Bond's ride to be something British, sleep, and sophisticated that wouldn't look out of place in a country club parking lot. Not one of Aston Martin's more hard-core variants but a gentleman's express with four seats, an opponent interior, and a plush ride. Probably Aston, maybe Range Rover, possible Rolls Royce.

Bond should drive a 5th gen Civic Type R. It was built in Britain, so it's got that covered.

However, he's a spy. He needs to maintain a low profile. Hence, Civic.

It's got to be an Aston Martin. It can't be the Valkyrie or the Valhalla. Those are too hard for the "Bond girl" to get in and out of in a dress. The Valen and the Valiant are both limited editions and would make good movie cars, but they're both a little too boy-racer for Bond. At the end of the day, a DB12 is the Bond car. It's long and lean, it has lots of room for gadgets, it's got class for days, and it's got a screaming V12 for when things get spirited. You can fight bad guys in it, then roll up to the opera.

Edit – Thanks to DetroitDawg for pointing out that the DB12 is a V8. I was thinking of the Vanquish.

Depends on the tone of the movie. If he's looking to drive something outrageous and have a 200mph chase, he'll drive a new Aston Martin Valhalla.

Something sophisticated to take to somewhere in a European city where you can only enter by birthright due to your great-great-great-grandfather saving someone in a war, the Aston Martin Valen.
